title: The Career-Change Resume: Leading With Transferable Skills When You Switch Industries
summary: Switching industries? Translate your experience into the new field: lead with transferable skills, write a bridging summary, and reframe every bullet.
body_text: How do you write a resume when you switch industries? Translate, don't just list. Take the experience you already have and rewrite it in the language of the field you want. Lead with the skills that carry over. Name the switch in a two-line summary up top so the recruiter knows what you are aiming at. Then reword each bullet to mirror the target job posting, because a reviewer in the new field sizes up your fit in seconds. Skip the pure skills-only "functional" layout, which recruiters read as hiding something. A hybrid works better: skills up front, real dated work history underneath. One honest caveat. The resume gets you read, but a hard pivot is usually won by your story and your network. Here is the part nobody tells you about changing fields. Your resume is probably not bad. It is written in a language the new reader does not speak, and that is a fixable problem. You spent years doing work that mattered, and every bullet on the page proves it, in the vocabulary of the industry you are leaving. A hiring manager in the field you want gives it maybe six or seven seconds. In that window they are answering one question: does this person's background map to my role? If your page is a wall of unfamiliar titles, tools, and acronyms, they stall. Not because you cannot do the job. Because you left them to connect the dots, and busy people do not. So the whole task of a career-change resume comes down to translation. You are not inventing experience or padding anything. You are taking real work and rewriting it so the overlap with the target role is impossible to miss. Get that right and the switch stops reading like a gamble on you. It starts reading like the obvious next step. Why your current resume reads like a foreign language Think about someone who ran logistics for a decade. They coordinated vendors, chased deadlines across teams, kept a dozen moving parts from colliding, and did it under pressure. On paper, their resume says "logistics," and it lists logistics things. But the work they actually did? That is project management with a different label. The resume is telling a story about shipping and warehouses when it should be telling a story about managing chaos across teams and deadlines. Same skillset. Different wrapper. That gap between what you did and how it reads is the single biggest reason career-change resumes get passed over. Recruiters do not sit with your resume and reverse-engineer your value. They pattern-match. When the pattern on your page is a field they are not hiring for, the easy call is to move on to the candidate who already speaks the language. Your job is to remove that friction so the reviewer never has to guess what you would bring. Lead with what actually carries over Before you touch a single bullet, figure out what genuinely transfers. Not the polite version where everything is a "transferable skill" if you squint. The real overlap. Some skills travel across almost any field: managing projects and stakeholders, analyzing data, owning a budget, writing clearly, coaching people, running a process without dropping balls. Others are more specific but still portable. Teaching becomes training and enablement. Sales becomes customer success. Operations becomes program or product coordination. A regulatory specialist who used to be the lab expert is now the person coordinating four to seven cross-functional leads in a room, which is its own high-value skill once you frame it that way. The move is to surface those skills high on the page, before the unfamiliar job titles make the reader stall. A skills-forward top section does the heavy lifting: it tells the recruiter what you bring in words they already use, so by the time they reach your old titles, they are reading them as evidence, not as a red flag. For the mechanics of building that block well, our guide to the skills section on a resume covers what belongs there and what is filler. One honest caveat. "Great communicator" and "strong collaborator" mean nothing on their own, and recruiters read them as wallpaper. A skill only counts when you prove it. Do not write that you translate between teams. Show the moment you took a technical mess and made it legible to a room of non-experts, and let the reader draw the conclusion. Write a bridging summary that names the switch Career-changers love to hide the pivot, as if a reviewer will not notice. They notice. What actually helps is naming it, on purpose, right at the top. A bridging summary is two or three lines that say what you are moving toward and what you carry into it. Keep it plain: "Operations lead moving into product, bringing five years of cross-functional delivery and a data habit to a team building X." One sentence, and it reframes everything under it. Your old work suddenly reads like preparation for this move instead of a detour away from it. The blunt version recruiters keep repeating: make it future-focused. If you are done being a teacher, stop marketing yourself as a former teacher. From the first two lines, it should be obvious what kind of role you are aiming at. A reviewer who cannot tell what you are applying for does not lean in with curiosity. They put the resume down. Frame the background as something you are adding to, not leaving behind. A service technician moving into a customer-facing tech role is not starting over. They are adding a technical layer to years of explaining hard things to frustrated people and earning their trust. That framing is honest, and it is a lot more convincing than pretending the last decade did not happen. If you want to go deeper on the wording, this resume summary for a career change breaks down the formula line by line. Translate your bullets, don't just corporate-ify them This is where most career-change resumes quietly fail, and it is worth slowing down. The common mistake looks a lot like effort. You take your existing bullets, swap "taught" for "facilitated," bolt a percentage onto the end, and figure you have translated them. You have not. All you have done is make your old job sound more corporate while it still describes your old job. The reviewer reads a nicely dressed version of the wrong story and moves on. Real translation is more ruthless than that. Take every bullet and ask it a yes-or-no question: is this about the skill I am pivoting into? If the answer is no, it does not earn a spot near the top, however proud of it you happen to be. Treat the resume as a targeted argument for one specific role rather than a summary of everything you have ever done. A teacher moving into project management does not dress up every classroom duty in business words and call it a day. They pull out the parts that were project management all along, and the rest gets trimmed hard. Then reword what survives in the target field's vocabulary. Read the job posting closely and mirror its language. If the role keeps saying "cross-functional coordination" and "roadmap," and you did exactly that under different words, use their words. This is the same literal keyword-mirroring that federal and military resume-writers rely on, and it matters here for the same reason: military-to-civilian resumes are the purest version of this problem, translating a whole vocabulary at once, but any industry switch is the same job on a smaller scale. Lead each bullet with the outcome, not the task. "Responsible for onboarding" is a job description; "Cut onboarding time by reworking the intake process" is a result someone will remember. And when you do not have a clean number to attach, you can still show scale and the change you drove. Our piece on how to quantify achievements without numbers is built for exactly the roles where a tidy revenue figure does not exist. Here is a quick before-and-after to make it concrete. Old field, buried: "Managed classroom of 30 students and coordinated with parents and administration." Translated for a coordinator role: "Ran a 30-person group through a structured yearly plan, kept administrators and families on the same page about progress, and adapted the plan mid-cycle when results lagged." Same work. Now a hiring manager who has never set foot in a school can see the coordination skill immediately. Translate, don't fabricate There is a line here, and it is worth drawing hard, because the whole method depends on it. Reframing real work is fair game. Inventing work is not, and it backfires faster than people think. Recruiters compare your claims against each other and against what they can verify. If a skill suddenly appears for a target role but was nowhere in the same job when you described it elsewhere, that inconsistency reads as a lie, and it kills the application on the spot. It is the resume equivalent of the sitcom character who claims he "sold five million units" of something. Everyone in the room already knows it is not true. Translation is turning "wrote curriculum" into "designed a structured learning program with defined outcomes," because that is literally what you did. Claiming you managed a budget you never touched is a different thing entirely, and it is the version that gets you caught when the details do not line up. When you are tempted to stretch, that is usually a sign to find the real transferable win you have been underselling instead. Does your resume still read like your old job? Run it through a free review to see where the old-field language is hiding, then rebuild it around the skills that carry over. Review my resume → What to cut and what to compress Space on a career-change resume is expensive, and most people spend it defending the field they are leaving. Flip that. Cut the old-industry-only jargon, the acronyms, and the prestige markers that only mean something inside your former bubble. For career-changers coming out of academia, the fix is blunt: talk about business outcomes and cut the academic material, because nobody outside higher ed cares which famous professor taught the course you built. The same holds for any field. The certifications, tools, and titles that impressed people in your old world often register as noise in the new one. Shrink the roles that do not support the pivot. You do not have to delete a decade, but an unrelated job can drop to a single line: title, employer, dates, done. Anything that anchors you hard to the field you are exiting, when it does not also make your case for the new one, is working against you. Every line you free up is a line you can spend on the transferable story. One caution on register. Match the tone of the place you are aiming at. If the target org values theory and rigor, keep some of that language. If it runs on speed and outcomes, strip it. The resume should read like it belongs in the field you want, and getting that wrong is a quiet way to self-select out before anyone even calls. Format honestly: skip the pure functional resume Somewhere along the way, career-changers get told to use a functional resume, the skills-only format that leads with capabilities and hides or removes the dated work history. On paper it sounds perfect for a pivot. In practice it is a trap. Recruiters distrust functional resumes, and the reason is simple: when someone buries their timeline, the reviewer assumes they are hiding something. A gap. A short tenure. A lack of recent experience in anything relevant. Even when you have nothing to hide, the format itself raises the question. On top of that, pure skills-only layouts tend to parse badly through applicant tracking software, which expects dated roles in reverse order. You can read the honest case for and against the functional resume format before you commit to it, but for most industry switches, it costs more trust than it saves. The safer modern choice is a hybrid. Keep a strong, skills-forward summary and skills section at the top, then give the reviewer a normal reverse-chronological work history underneath. You get the best of the pivot resume, your capabilities lead the page, without erasing your timeline or spooking a recruiter. Skills-forward, not skills-only. That distinction is the whole game. Yes, the software still reads your career-change resume People assume the parsing rules relax for career-changers. They do not. Your resume goes through the same applicant tracking systems as everyone else's, so the format hygiene still matters: a single column, real selectable text instead of images, no tables or text boxes or graphics that scramble the parse, and no critical information stranded in a header or footer. Two things matter more when you are switching. First, put a tailored skills block near the top with the exact wording from the target posting, because that is what a keyword match keys on. Second, do not panic about the software. The tracking system is a filing cabinet with a search bar, not a bouncer deciding your fate. If you want to see how yours actually reads, our walkthrough on how to test whether a resume is ATS-friendly shows the free ways to check, and our ATS auto-reject myth piece explains why the scarier rumors are mostly wrong. A pivot is more than a new job title It helps to be clear about what you are actually doing, because two different situations get lumped together and they need different resumes. If you are staying in your field and reframing a title, say your company called you a "Customer Success Ninja" and you want it to read as "Account Manager" on your resume, that is a retitling problem. You are keeping the same experience and giving it a standard, searchable name. That is a real and useful move, and it has its own rules, which we cover in changing a job title on your resume . An industry switch is bigger. You are re-aiming your entire experience at a field where your old titles carry no weight, not simply renaming one role. The transferable-skills workflow in this guide is for that harder case. If your switch is really a retitle in disguise, use the lighter fix and save yourself the effort. The honest limit: a resume gets you read, not hired Now the part that most career-change advice skips, because it is not what people want to hear. A great career-change resume gets you past the paper screen. It rarely wins a hard pivot on its own. When you move to a genuinely new industry, plenty of hiring managers treat you like a new graduate, no matter how strong your old career was, because prior experience in their field is still what they weigh most. That is not fair, but it is the room you are walking into, and pretending otherwise sets you up to be discouraged when the applications go quiet. So the resume is necessary, not sufficient. The switch usually gets won by three other things. The first is the story, the "why this move, why now," which a resume cannot carry but a targeted cover letter can. If you are making a real pivot, put that reasoning somewhere a human will read it, and write it like a person rather than a template. Our reusable cover letter template and the piece on sending it as an email cover letter both help you say it without sounding stiff. The second is people. A cold application into a hard pivot is the slowest path in. The fastest is a warm one, a referral, a former colleague, an alum from your program, someone who will walk your resume past the pile. The consistent advice for a hard pivot is to spend real time on the network, not only on the applications. The third is patience with the path. Sometimes the clean jump does not exist and a bridge role does: recruiting for the industry you are leaving, taking an adjacent title that touches the new field, or accepting a rung lower to get a foot in the door. A film production manager who got a project-coordinator job through a certification did not land their dream role. They got into a field with steady hours and a real title, and then they had new-field experience to build on. Call it a route in rather than a compromise. Tailor per role, and get an outside read Two habits separate the career-changers who get interviews from the ones who send fifty applications into silence. Tailor every time. You cannot mass-blast one career-change resume across a dozen roles, because the whole point of translation is aiming your experience at a specific target. It does not take long, ten to fifteen minutes to mirror a posting's language and reorder your skills for it, but it is not optional. A generic pivot resume reads as generic to every reader. And get someone else to look at it. You are too close to your own history to see the jargon anymore; the acronyms and shorthand that scream "old field" are invisible to you because they are just how you think. An outside reader, or a review tool that flags the gap between your resume and a target posting, catches the language you cannot. If you would rather build the whole thing on a structure that keeps the skills-forward format intact while you tailor, you can build your career-change resume and adjust it per role without breaking the layout. And if you want the wider view of how your application moves once it is out the door, our overview of how hiring actually works maps the whole path from apply to offer. Switching fields is hard enough without your resume working against you. Translate the experience you already have, lead with the overlap, and be honest about what the resume can and cannot do. It gets you in the door. You do the rest. Frequently Asked Questions Should I use a functional resume for a career change? Probably not. The pure skills-only version hides your dated work history, and to a recruiter, a buried timeline reads as something to hide. That costs you trust before they reach a single bullet. It parses badly too, since the software wants roles in reverse order. Go hybrid: skills up front, real history underneath. Our functional resume breakdown lays out the full trade-off. What are transferable skills, exactly? The abilities that keep their value when you cross into a new field. Project and stakeholder management. Data analysis, budgeting, clear writing, coaching, owning a process from start to finish. A few are field-specific but still portable, like teaching that becomes training, or sales that becomes customer success. Here is the test: could you do this in the target role next week? If yes, put it high and back it with one real example. Where do I put the career change on my resume? Right at the top. A two or three line summary that names what you are moving toward and what you carry into it. Do not tuck the pivot away and hope nobody clocks it. When a recruiter cannot tell which role you are chasing, they usually move on. Say it plainly, then let that summary decide what you lead with below. How do I rewrite my bullets for a new industry? Run each one through a single yes-or-no question. Is this bullet about the skill I am pivoting into? If not, it gets cut or shrunk. Whatever survives, reword it in the target field's vocabulary, and pull the exact phrases straight from the job posting. Lead with the result rather than the duty. You are not changing what you did, only the words a new reader will recognize. Is reframing my experience the same as lying? No, provided you translate real work instead of inventing it. "Wrote curriculum" becoming "designed a structured learning program with defined outcomes" is fair game. That is what you did. Claiming a budget you never touched is not, and recruiters spot the inconsistency quickly when the story does not line up. Feeling the urge to stretch usually means there is a genuine win nearby that you have been underselling. Should I cut old jobs that don't relate to my new field? Compress, do not delete. An unrelated role can drop to one line: title, employer, dates. That keeps your timeline intact, which recruiters like to see, and it hands you space for the transferable story instead. What you should actually cut is the old-field jargon, the acronyms, and the prestige markers that mean nothing to anyone outside your former industry. Does the ATS treat a career-change resume differently? It does not. Your resume runs through the same applicant tracking software as everyone else's, so the usual rules hold: one column, real text, no tables or graphics, nothing important stranded in a header. The one thing that matters more for a switch is a tailored skills block near the top, worded to match the posting. Want to see how yours reads? You can test how it parses for free. Can I change careers without going back to school? Frequently, yes. It works when you can prove the transferable skills and the target role does not legally require a credential. Plenty of switches ride on reframed experience plus a short certificate or some focused self-study to close one gap, no full degree needed. School helps in fields that gatekeep on it. For a lot of pivots, though, it is not the thing that decides the outcome. Your resume and your network usually are. Is a resume enough to change industries? Rarely, on its own, for a hard pivot. It gets you read, which matters, but many hiring managers still weigh field experience heavily. What actually moves the needle is the full package: a translated resume, a targeted cover letter that explains why you are switching, and real networking to get a warm introduction. Sometimes the realistic first step is a bridge or adjacent role. Treat the resume as necessary, not as the whole plan. Do I need a different resume for every role I apply to? For a career change, yes. Translation only does its job when it is aimed at one specific target, so you mirror each posting's language and reorder your skills to fit. That is ten or fifteen minutes of work per role, not a rewrite from scratch. Send the same generic pivot resume everywhere and it reads as generic everywhere, which is the last thing you want when you are already the unfamiliar name in the pile. title: How to Optimize Your Digital Checkout for Better Conversion Rates
summary: Achieve better conversion rate & revenue flow by optimising digital checkouts. Here's an ultimate guide for Payments Product Managers.
body_text: Table of Contents Toggle A checkout process is ultimately where a marketer’s spending will produce revenue, or disappear. According to Baymard Institute’s ongoing research , cart abandonment rate exceeds 70%, and checkout friction represents a significant portion of that problem. For a payment products manager, that rate is a clear call-to-action. A checkout audit is not something optional. That is the fastest path to identifying where money is leaking out without changing spend for acquiring products, or adjusting your product offerings. Cashfree payments has been processing online payments since nearly a decade ago. This guide provides practical applications based upon our experience at Cashfree Payments, broken down into three parts of the payment journey: pre-payment, checkout and post-payment. 6 Principles of Checkout Optimization 1. Faster checkout Baymard institute research on cart abandonment consistently places slow or confusing checkouts as one of the leading reasons shoppers walk away from completing a purchase. Every second longer at checkout costs you. Customers don’t wait around to change their minds. Once a customer has completed a fast checkout , they have no window in which to reconsider and leave. Maintaining intent high throughout the checkout process is important, and prevents customers from changing their mind about making the purchase. 2. Fewer inputs Customer Convenience beats almost all other factors during the checkout process. Forcing account creation before purchase is a proven conversion killer. Baymard institute research lists creating an account before making a purchase among the top causes of abandoned carts with drop off rates tied directly to this single friction point exceeding 20 percent. Ask yourself only one question for each field on your form: “does this input block the payment from being made?” if the answer is “no” remove the field. 3. Inputs should be Validated A majority of purchases online today are done via mobile. Even in the best of times, typing in addresses, card numbers, UPI VPAs , or net banking details carries a high probability of input errors. If the input is not validated as it is entered, users will face a payment failure. 33% of those users who experience a failed payment will abandon the checkout entirely, thereby lowering the conversion rate. Validating inputs (a small “Card number not valid” below the card number field) can prompt customers to review their information. Thus, this will avoid a payment failure for customers and safeguard your revenue better. 4. The Right Information at the Right Time If you don’t support a particular kind of card network or are having issues with a particular payment mode, let the user know before they try to make the payment and the payment fails. This will help avoid a negative user experience, cart abandonment and poor conversion rate. It is more likely to ensure that a user completes the checkout and makes the payment. 5. Personalisation Helps – A Lot! Saved preferences turn transactions into relationships. A returning customer who sees their preferred UPI app or saved card selected by default completes checkout Faster, and feels recognized. Use a subscription business example to illustrate this. A customer who has paid using UPI three times in a row should not need to select a payment method again. Display the first option, the one they previously used, by default. 6. Accessibility is Essential Accessibility isn’t optional, it’s a conversion lever. Screen reader compatibility, adequate colour contrast, keyboard-only navigation allow more of your traffic to complete purchase. At minimum, ensure that checkouts support alt text on all payment icons and logos, visible focus states for keyboard users, and resizing text without breaking layout. Ignore these options and you’ll quietly discourage a segment of your paying customers from proceeding through your checkout process. Now that we’ve discussed these principles, let’s have a look at an annotated checklist that details best practices in the 3 stages of pre-payment, checkout, and post-payment to maximise conversion rates, reduce cart abandonment, and give a great payment experience to your customers. Pre-Payment Checklist Are you showcasing offers, discounts, EMIs, and Pay Later options on the product display page? Customers decide to buy based upon the value they perceive. When product pages present offers, discounts and Pay Later options prior to starting the checkout process order values and conversions are higher, according to multiple industry checkout studies including baymard institute research on transparency during the pre-purchase phase. Is a guest checkout accessible? Up to 35% of digital shoppers will abandon their cart if forced to make an account on an e-commerce website. So, having a guest checkout keeps your conversion rate high . You can always prompt the users to sign up once they place the order. Are you requiring users to log in? If so, is login enabled via OTP? Most users will find it easier to log in via an OTP than to remember a username and a password. Therefore, always keep the ‘login via OTP ‘ option available to make it more convenient for your customers to complete the transaction. Are you only taking inputs that are absolutely essential? The more effort the user has to make, the lower your conversion rate will be. Keep the inputs you take prior to payment to the bare minimum . For instance, just a phone number/email if no physical delivery is required . Just that and the address where it is ! Keep asking yourself if this input is required to complete the payment. So, only have that input there if it meets that bar. Is there a progress bar or some indicators that users can see how many more steps there are? ~70% of users abandon carts somewhere in the middle of the purchase process. In many instances, this is due to frustration at long checkouts. Thus, having a progress bar will let your customers know how much longer it’ll take them to complete the checkout. This can reduce cart abandonment by 10-20%. Do you have an exit intent pop-up to avoid cart abandonment? Most internet users (rightly!) hate the pop-ups. However, an exit-intent pop-up with some good copy and social proof can help increase your conversion rate by 2-3% by preventing last-minute cart abandonment. Checkout Checklist Overall Are preferred or saved payment modes visible to all users? Payment mode visibility is important, but absolutely essential when dealing with returning customers. Showing them their preferred payment mode reduces the time taken to check out. Hence, it increases the convenience to the users – resulting in a higher conversion rate and a better customer experience. Are all offers and discounts accessible to users? Offers and discounts (including EMI and Pay Later options) are essential to increasing your conversion rate. By lowering the effective price paid front-up by the prospective customer, there is a higher probability of the customer completing the purchase. Unfortunately, a majority of checkouts have offers visible only after they are already on the payments page. [Check BNPL Plus – Display Pay later options, EMIs and offers on the product page – Boost conversions by 40%] If the user is a returning/logged-in user, are you asking for their phone number again? This is an important way that you can reduce user friction. Pass the user’s phone number from your system to the payment aggregator in an API call instead of forcing the user to enter it again to finalize the payment. So, this will make the payment flow smoother and increase the conversion rate. In case of downtimes or payment failures, are you prompting users to leverage an alternate payment method? Payment failures cause 33% of your users to drop once they have experienced them. So, it is better to warn them beforehand. Adding a warning that a particular method is facing low success rates and prompting users to leverage another method will substantially lower cart abandonment for your business. Thus, the conversion rate may not dip. Card Payments Are Credit Cards and Debit Cards enabled on your checkout? This is a basic hygiene check if you want to keep your conversion rate high. Most businesses today should offer these modes of digital payments because they drive a substantial volume of total transactions. Needless to say, the highest-spending cohort of digital customers in India use cards. Are all 6 major networks – (Rupay, Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Maestro, Diner’s Club) available? Having all the major card networks available on your checkout will make for a better customer experience. This is because they will be able to use the payment method of their choice. Are all the card networks available shown via their logos? Visually depicting the card network logos will make sure that customers know which networks are available at your checkout. This will reduce payment failures and therefore, cart abandonments. Do you offer a saved card experience, compliant with RBI’s Tokenisation guidelines? A saved card experience makes it easier for a customer to pay when they return to your checkout. Therefore, it drives better retention for your business – especially for high-value customers. Are all card inputs – card number, expiry date, etc. – validated? Typing in card details can be tricky, and involves entering 15-20 digits. On a mobile checkout, this can be tricky and is prone to error. A validation check will prompt the user to check their details before they proceed to the next step. This will make it more likely that they will complete the transaction. Do you offer CVV-free payments on saved cards? A CVV-free payment experience will drive a 10-15% higher success rate. It will reduce cart abandonment by making the checkout process that much easier and faster. Thus, the conversion rate will also improve. Do you offer NFC-enabled card details auto-fill on your checkout? Since entering card details can be tricky, it is best to reduce that friction by automatically fetching these details. It will be more convenient for customers. Leveraging Near Field Communication (NFC) technology, today’s smartphones can auto-fetch card details if customers hold the cards above the smartphone. Thus, it becomes seamless to enter these details. You should definitely have this on your checkout if you want to shoot up your conversion rate. UPI Payments On web checkout – are you offering a UPI QR code scanning experience? Even those transacting on your website via their desktops will need their mobile phones to complete UPI payments. A UPI QR code to scan makes it much easier for them to complete the payment on their smartphones. On mobile/app checkout – are you offering a UPI Intent flow? UPI Intent is the most preferred way to pay with UPI on digital checkouts. It offers a substantial improvement in both success rate and user experience compared to UPI Collect. Are you using an SDK to show the user the apps installed on their phone? UPI Intent is made more effective with an SDK that automatically throws up the user’s currently installed UPI PSPs. This increases conversion rates and customer satisfaction. Are you validating and verifying UPI IDs when they are entered? UPI Collect is still used by a substantial number of users to complete their UPI checkout. Having a VPA validation and verification avoids payment failures. Do you offer In-app UPI flows? In-app UPI is the fastest-ever and most failure-free way for customers to pay via UPI on digital checkouts . By removing the need to be redirected to a UPI PSP and only requiring the entry of a UPI PIN, businesses such as yours can offer the fastest and most conversion-friendly checkout experience to their customers. Netbanking Payments Is Netbanking enabled on your checkout? Netbanking is not a very popular payment method. Nevertheless, customers often pref er it when they are making large purchases since this avoids UPI payment or credit card limits. Does your bank list showcase the top banks? It is most effective to place the most popular banks at the top of your net banking flow. There are well over 70 banks in India that offer digital net banking services, but the top 6 banks hold >80% of all accounts. Placing them up front will make the checkout process more convenient for customers, which can improve the conversion rate. Do you have >70 banks available? Having a wide variety of banks available in net banking ensures that you can serve all customers, even if they hold an account with a relatively unfamiliar bank. So, make sure that you have a broad selection of banks available. Are you offering EMIs on Netbanking? Some banks are now offering EMIs on Netbanking. This can be a conversion and order value enhancer for net banking users. So , it is something your business should have to maximize the potential for converting these customers. Wallet Payments Have you enabled digital wallets on your checkout? Digital wallets continue to be a favoured payment mode for some customers, and you should have them available at your checkout. Do you have >7 wallets available on your checkout? The top 7 wallets contribute ~80-90% of the transactions processed in the digital wallet ecosystem. Having more than that will ensure that most people wanting to pay via a digital wallet will have the ability to choose a wallet of their choice. Is wallet link-and-pay available on your checkout? Wallet link-and-pay enables users to make one-click payments via digital wallets on your checkout, basically saving the wallet as a payment method. This is useful for digital wallet users. Are the top wallets showcased on top of your list? Most users prefer one wallet on which they have a loaded value. Therefore, it is important that they can access the wallet they wish to use easily. Having your list of wallets represented by their use can improve accessibility and enhance the checkout conversion rate. Card/Cardless EMI Payments Are CC, DC, and Cardless EMIs enabled on your checkout? Credit Cards, Debit Cards, and Cardless EMIs drive considerable volumes, especially for high-value items and premium SKUs. This includes furniture, electronics, When customers enter valid Credit/Debit card numbers, is there a prompt that shows EMIs are available? Input validation checks prevent payment failures resulting from incorrect entry of credit card numbers. Placing a validation check here can ensure that customers correct typographical errors as they happen. Is there an eligibility check flow for EMI payments? Eligibility checks are critical for customers who are trying EMIs for the first time. These checks let the users know whether or not they can use EMIs. Hence, it prevents them from abandoning the cart due to an error message. Are the EMI terms clearly called out (instalment, duration, interest, etc.)? Giving this visibility to EMI users lowers abandonment. The lack of this information will make a user reluctant to complete the transaction. Are you showcasing the top providers? Your checkout should default to showing the top card and cardless EMI providers to make it more accessible to customers using this payment mode. Pay Later O ptions Have you enabled Pay Later options on your checkout? Pay Later options are new-age solutions for credit seekers who either don’t have or don’t wish to use their bank account-linked instruments to avail quick and easy credit at checkout. You should enable this on your checkout, especially if you have high-value or premium SKUs at a high price point (>₹1000). Is there an eligibility check flow for BNPL providers? For those who are new to availing of the Pay Later options, an eligibility check will quickly let them know whether or not such options are available to them. This will drive a higher success rate and a better user experience. Are the Pay Later terms clearly called out (instalment, duration, interest, etc.)? Giving this visibility to Pay Later prospects drives lower abandonment. The lack of this information will make a user reluctant to complete the transaction. Are you showcasing the top providers? Your checkout should default to showing the top BNPL providers to make the more popular options accessible to customers using this payment mode. Post- P ayment Checklist In case of failed payments – Is there a retry prompt? At the point of a payment failure, 33% of users churn and abandon checkout. Having a quick retry prompt tends to reduce churn caused by payment failure, and reduces your cost of customer acquisition. Is the reason clearly indicated for user convenience? If a payment fails but no reason is provided, it makes the user not understand what has gone wrong. With ~80% of all payment failures connected to user action, it is much more effective to indicate the reason (incorrect CVV, etc.) in language that the user can understand. Are you suggesting the right next step? (i.e., if customers enter the incorrect CVV, are you letting them know that the CVV was incorrect and that they should try again with the same card?) This is connected to the previous point. If there has been a user error, the user should be prompted to correct that and complete checkout. If there is downtime or if the mode is showing low success rates, you should prompt the user to try another payment mode. If customers do not retry the payment, do you send an SMS/E-mail/both with a payment link? This is a tried and tested way to recover abandoned carts and drive up your overall conversion rate. By sending communications to churned prospects, you are far more likely to get a conversion because your intent has been expressed. In case of successful payments – Is there a payment successful and order confirmation screen? It is important to let the user know that their payment was successful and the order was confirmed. Is the user then being redirected back to the right place in your ecosystem? This varies depending on the type of business you are in. For example, with a food order, the next screen post the order confirmation should show delivery timelines and give a brief summary of the order. Is the user then being redirected back to the right place in your ecosystem? Sending an email/SMS confirmation helps users track their orders and ensures a complete user experience. We hope that you found this useful. If you want to have a free audit conducted of your checkout and payment flow, the experts at Cashfree Payments would be more than happy to help you. Click the button below to express your intent for a payments audit in the form below, and our experts will be in touch. get your free Payments AUDIT TODAY! FAQs What is Checkout Optimization? Checkout optimization refers to reducing friction within a merchant’s checkout flow to allow more shoppers who begin checking out to ultimately finish doing so. Examples of checkout optimizations include optimizing forms for easier input, providing multiple choices for payment types, improving page load speeds, and providing various trust indicators. What is a good checkout conversion rate? A good checkout conversion rate is defined as being above 70% for completing the checkout flow when reaching the payment screen; while below 50% indicates there is substantial friction present in the flow that needs to be audited. Is offering guest checkout better than forcing account creation prior to checkout? Forcing shoppers to create an account prior to making a purchase is one of the most commonly cited reasons for shopping cart abandonment. Provide guest checkout as the default option and ask the shopper if they would like to create an account after the order has been confirmed, rather than requiring them to do so before purchasing. How many payment methods does a checkout need to provide? You want to provide enough payment methods to satisfy your customer base, but not overwhelm the payment screen. Typically for most businesses operating in India this includes cards, UPI, net banking and at least one type of wallet/ Pay Later option. How long should it take for a shopper to complete a checkout? If the shopper is logged in and their information is saved then under 90 seconds is acceptable. If the shopper is logging in as a new guest, then under three minutes is acceptable. Must mobile checkout have a different approach than desktop checkout? Yes. Shoppers using mobile devices require larger “tap” targets, autofill capabilities, and native mobile “payment” options such as UPI Intent vs. scaled down versions of desktop checkouts.

(NASDAQ: REKR) ("Rekor" or the "Company"), which builds trusted data, privacy, and security solutions for real-world video and sensor networks, reported financial and operational results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Revenue of $12.7 million, up 23% sequentially and 2% year over year. Recurring revenue increased 14% year over year to $6.7 million in Q2 and 21% to $13.3 million for the first six months of 2026. Adjusted gross margin of 56%, up from 50% in Q2 2025. Adjusted EBITDA loss of $1.2 million, a 79% improvement from Q2 2025. Cash used in operating activities improved 61% year over year for the first six months of 2026. Headcount decreased by 20% in the first half of 2026. Outlook: Adjusted EBITDA profitability expected during the second half of 2026. Product: Launched Go-Secure.Video and the Rekor Scout Axis Agent integration during the quarter. What Drove the Quarter Rekor reduced headcount by 20% during the first half of 2026 and realigned its engineering operations. Management has identified further efficiencies, unrelated to workforce which are expected to produce several million dollars of additional annualized savings. Second quarter revenue rose to $12.7 million, up 23% from the first quarter and 2% in the prior-year period. The increase did not include any large, non-recurring software transactions. It reflects the ongoing economics of the business as it is structured today and meaningful growth in the Company’s recurring revenue base. Adjusted gross margin improved to 56% from 50% in the second quarter of 2025. Higher-margin software and recurring revenue made up a larger share of total revenue, and greater deployment volume allowed the Company to operate more efficiently. Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $1.2 million, a 79% improvement over the second quarter of 2025. Lower payroll and payroll-related costs, together with revenue growth and improved gross margin, drove the Adjusted EBITDA improvement. Tighter working capital management also contributed to the improvement in operating cash consumption. "The second quarter highlights the financial impact of the operating changes we implemented during the first half of the year." said Joseph Nalepa, Chief Financial Officer, Rekor. "During the second quarter of 2026, Adjusted EBITDA loss improved by $4.6 million to a loss of $1.2 million. At the same time, recurring revenue continued to grow and we materially reduced our operating expense base. Taken together, these results demonstrate the operating leverage we believe exists in the business as we continue our progress toward Adjusted EBITDA profitability." Cash Position and Outlook: The Company ended the second quarter of 2026 with $10.0 million in cash. Operating cash burn for the quarter was $2.4 million. For the six months ended June 30, 2026, cash used in operating activities improved by $9.6 million, or 61%, compared with the prior-year period. The improvement reflects the Company’s lower operating expense base, improved gross profit and continued focus on working capital management. Management believes the reduction in cash consumption provides further evidence that the operational changes implemented during the first half of the year are translating into improved financial performance as the Company progresses toward Adjusted EBITDA profitability. The Company is also evaluating options to refinance its existing Prime Revenue Sharing Notes. The refinancing has been supported by increases in the size of Rekor's contract portfolio and improvements in operations. Three and Six Months Ended June 30, 2026 Financial Results This section highlights the changes for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026, compared to the three and six months ended June 30, 2025. Second-quarter revenue increased to $12.7 million, up about 2% from $12.4 million. First-half revenue rose to $22.9 million, up about 6% year over year. Importantly, recurring revenue increased 14% in the quarter and 21% for the first six months, reaching $6.7 million and $13.3 million, respectively. Adjusted gross profit increased for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026, while adjusted gross margin expanded from 50% to 56% for the three months ended June 30, 2026. For the first half, adjusted gross margin rose from 49% to 55%. This improvement reflects the benefits of revenue growth and product mix, as Adjusted Gross Margin is generally influenced by the proportion of higher-margin software sales relative to service-related work. Adjusted Gross Margin is a non-GAAP financial measure calculated as Adjusted Gross Profit divided by revenue and should not be considered in isolation from, or as a substitute for, GAAP financial measures. The Company’s operating performance improved meaningfully during the second quarter, reflecting revenue growth, higher Adjusted Gross Profit and the impact of organizational efficiency measures implemented earlier in the year. For the three and six months ended June 30, 2026, combined general and administrative, selling and marketing, and research and development expenses decreased by $4.0 million and $4.3 million, respectively, compared with the prior-year periods. title: AWS Transform for migrations automates post-launch actions
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with AWS Transform for migrations automates post-launch actions
body_text: AWS Transform now automates the configuration and execution of post-launch actions through the migration workflow. Define actions at the account level and apply them automatically to each source server across your target accounts, including multi-account migrations. Automating these actions removes the slow, error-prone work of configuring them server by server, so your team moves more servers with less hands-on effort. Post-launch actions run through AWS Systems Manager (SSM) immediately after test or cutover launch. You can use predefined actions or bring your own SSM document. For source server bulk configurations, the migration inventory file now includes a new structure for post-launch actions, making it easier to review and modify actions per source server. The AWS Transform for migrations agent automates your migration configuration end to end, including replication templates, EC2 launch templates, EC2 right-sizing, and post-launch actions, with the flexibility to create and edit any of these at the source server level. This new capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered . To learn more, please visit the AWS Transform User Guide .

title: Service-Led Growth Starts with the Business Model
summary: Service-led growth starts with a business model. Tech can help scale a service business but does not define how value's created or delivered.
body_text: Organizations often look at AI, automation, or new service tools as the starting point for service-led growth. In reality, service-led growth starts with a business model. Technology can help scale a service business, but it does not define how value is created, delivered, or monetized. Service-led growth is one of the seven macro trends within Autonomous CX, SAP’s vision introduced at SAP Sapphire in 2026. At its core is a simple principle: every customer promise must be backed by the operational reality needed to deliver it. Recent SAP research highlights a growing gap between customer expectations and the operational reality of service delivery. Disconnected handoffs, fragmented information, and pressure to adopt AI make service a business-model question, not just a technology one. A practitioner’s perspective More than twenty years ago, I was part of a global service organization that wanted to move beyond viewing service as a cost of doing business. At the time, our primary objective was cost recovery. Service was necessary to support the product business, but it was not really seen as a business in its own right. We started changing that by introducing new professional services and finding ways to monetize expertise we already had. Remote device monitoring, for example, allowed us to organize support across time zones and offer profitable after-hours services to customers who depended on continuous operations. Realize the transformative value of your investment with proactive guidance supported by AI Learn more A few years later, I was asked a more fundamental question: could the service organization survive as an independent business? To explore that question, we used an early version of what later became widely known as the business model canvas. We looked beyond service operations and examined the complete picture: our value proposition, customer segments, channels, activities, resources, costs, and revenue streams. Looking back, that exercise taught me something that is still relevant today. Service as a revenue driver is not a new idea. And it does not start with technology. It starts with a business model. What do we mean by service-led revenue? “Service as a revenue driver” is often used as if it means one thing. In reality, service can contribute to revenue in several different ways. First, it can protect revenue . A customer whose issue is resolved quickly and professionally is more likely to renew, continue buying, and remain loyal. Second, it can influence revenue . Service professionals often understand a customer’s operational reality better than anyone else. They may identify a need for additional services, training, upgrades, or new solutions, creating opportunities for commercial teams. Third, it can generate revenue directly through premium support, professional services, subscriptions, remote monitoring, advisory services, or outcome-based offerings. These ambitions are related, but they are not the same. Each requires different processes, skills, measures, and sometimes different operating models. Not every service interaction should become a sales conversation. But every service organization should understand whether it is expected to protect, influence, or directly generate revenue. Technology creates possibilities, not the business model Technology has always played an important role in service innovation. Remote monitoring reduced the need for on-site visits. Connected solutions made global support models possible. Customer and service platforms improved access to account, contract, equipment, and interaction data. Today, Autonomous CX capabilities can expand these possibilities even further. Joule, embedded AI agents in SAP Service Cloud, and AI-assisted opportunity detection in SAP Sales Cloud can classify and route cases, summarize interactions, surface relevant knowledge, identify patterns, detect revenue opportunities, and increasingly automate routine requests. All within the context of a connected service and sales operating model. Yet adoption does not equal usage, and usage does not equal value. Technology does not answer the most important questions: What value are customers willing to pay for? Which customers should we serve? How will the service be sold, delivered, and measured? Can it be delivered consistently, profitably, and adopted by employees and customers? Customers are already drawing their own conclusions. In 2026, 81% believe AI in service is deployed primarily to save money, not to improve service. Seventy-nine percent still strongly prefer human support. These perceptions are not only a trust problem, they point to a business model problem. When the technology decision precedes the value decision, customers notice. From ambition to execution This is where many service-led growth initiatives struggle. Ambition may be clear in the boardroom, while the organization underneath continues to operate as before. Service is still measured primarily on cost and case closure. Sales and service pursue different objectives. Customer information remains fragmented. Opportunities identified by service disappear during handovers. Employees are expected to adopt new behaviors without understanding why. Turning service into a measurable revenue driver therefore requires more than enabling a new feature or deploying a new technology. It requires alignment between business objectives, processes, people, data, and technology. The Advanced Success Plan version for SAP Customer Experience solutions is an expert-led engagement model that helps translate Autonomous CX into an executable plan. It does not replace business strategy or determine which services should be brought to market. Instead, it helps connect a chosen ambition to the processes, capabilities, and governance needed to make service-led growth measurable and repeatable. 1. Clarify the value intent The first step is to define what service-led growth actually means for the organization. Is the priority to improve retention? Increase renewals? Create opportunities through service interactions? Launch paid services? Improve profitability? Through the value management expert session within the Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience solutions, stakeholders can align on business priorities, value drivers, and success measures. The objective is not to create a long list of KPIs, but a shared understanding of the outcomes that matter most. 2. Connect the end-to-end process Once the ambition is clear, the next question is how value will actually be created. If a service professional identifies an opportunity, what happens next? Who owns the follow-up? Is the customer experience consistent from the initial interaction through fulfilment and invoicing? Business process best practices and expert guidance can help identify gaps in ownership, handovers, and process alignment across service, sales, commerce, and supporting operations. This matters beyond operational efficiency. SAP research shows that 45% of revenue leaders cite improving collaboration and handoffs across marketing, sales, and service as a current priority, and 39% are actively pursuing expansion, cross-selling, and upselling within existing accounts. Service teams often have valuable customer context, but the real question is whether the process exists to act on it. 3. Close capability and adoption gaps Organizations can then assess which capabilities are needed to support the process. This could involve better access to customer information, improved knowledge management, analytics, automation, AI-supported recommendations, or opportunity management capabilities. Targeted expert services within the Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience solutions help connect SAP CX capabilities to desired business outcomes. At the same time, employees need the right enablement, incentives, and confidence to adopt new ways of working. Without that, even the best-designed process remains a PowerPoint slide. The cost of getting this wrong is real. Employees asked to adopt new behaviors without understanding why, or without the tools to support them, do not persist. When experienced people leave, they take institutional knowledge and customer relationships with them. Enablement is not a training exercise; it is a retention and continuity investment. 4. Measure, learn, and improve Service-led growth is not delivered through a single project. Recent research highlights several recurring priorities for service leaders: efficiency and time to resolution (48%), collaboration and handoffs across marketing, sales, and service (46%), first-contact resolution (40%), and AI-driven predictive insights (33%). These figures provide useful context, but the measures that matter for service-led growth depend on the value intent defined at the start. Progress should therefore be tracked against the agreed outcomes, whether these involve retention, renewals, service-generated opportunities, paid-service revenue, or profitability. Ongoing governance and engagement planning helps organizations review progress, address gaps, and scale successful approaches over time. Service-led growth is a business-model choice Moving from cost recovery to service-led growth is not simply a matter of asking service employees to sell more. It is a business-model choice with implications for the value proposition, customer experience, processes, organization, skills, technology, and measures of success. Twenty years ago, remote monitoring changed what service organizations could deliver. Today, AI is expanding those possibilities again. But the underlying challenge has not changed. Technology changes possibilities. Business models determine how that value is captured. First, decide where service should create value. Then, build the operating model required to deliver that value consistently and profitably. The Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience solutions can support that journey by helping organizations connect business outcomes with the processes, capabilities, adoption, and governance needed to turn ambition into measurable results. title: Guía completa del Régimen RESICO 2026
summary: RESICO te permite pagar entre 1% y 2.5% de ISR en lugar del 20-35% del régimen general. Esta guía te explica quién califica, cuánto pagas, tus obligaciones y los errores que te pueden sacar del régimen.
body_text: RESICO existe desde 2022, y la mayoría de las personas que califican no lo saben. O peor: ya están en él, pero no entienden cómo funciona. Esta guía te explica todo lo que necesitas saber. Dato clave: Un freelancer que gana $45,000 al mes paga $495 de ISR en RESICO. En el régimen general pagaría alrededor de $7,000. Eso es un ahorro de más de $78,000 al año. ¿Qué es RESICO? RESICO es un régimen fiscal para personas físicas que ganan hasta $3,500,000 al año. En lugar de calcular deducciones, coeficientes y tablas complicadas, simplemente pagas un porcentaje fijo sobre lo que cobras en el mes. Ejemplo: si cobraste $30,000 en un mes, tu ISR es $330. Sin fórmula escondida. Sin cuota fija. Ese porcentaje va del 1% al 2.5%, dependiendo de cuánto ganes. Está regulado en los artículos 113-E a 113-J de la Ley del ISR. Tasas bajas. Del 1% al 2.5% de ISR, dependiendo de tu nivel de ingreso mensual. Cálculo simple. Porcentaje directo sobre lo que cobras. Sin fórmulas complicadas. Sin papeleo extra. No llevas contabilidad electrónica, no envías balanzas, no presentas DIOT. Sin declaración anual. Desde 2026, tus pagos mensuales son definitivos. El SAT ya no te la pide. ¿Quién puede estar en RESICO? Ingresos anuales: hasta $3,500,000 MXN Tipo de actividad: empresarial, servicios profesionales o arrendamiento RFC activo y actualizado ante el SAT e.firma vigente (obligatoria desde enero 2026) Buzón tributario habilitado con correo electrónico verificado Facturación: emitir CFDI por todos tus ingresos sin excepción Perfiles que califican: diseñadores, programadores, consultores, coaches, contadores, abogados, arquitectos, psicólogos, dueños de tiendas o negocios con ventas menores a $3.5M, y personas que rentan inmuebles. ¿Quién NO puede estar en RESICO? Socios o accionistas de una empresa (persona moral) Conductores de Uber, DiDi, Rappi o cualquier plataforma tecnológica Miembros de consejos directivos, de vigilancia o consultivos Personas que ya fueron dadas de baja de RESICO por incumplimiento Residentes en el extranjero con establecimiento en México Dato importante: Si eres freelancer y además manejas Uber los fines de semana, pierdes RESICO para TODOS tus ingresos. ¿Cuánto pagas en RESICO? La tasa se aplica sobre la totalidad de lo que cobraste en el mes. No es tasa marginal: todo tu ingreso paga la misma tasa. Hasta $25,000: 1.00% De $25,001 a $50,000: 1.10% De $50,001 a $83,333: 1.50% De $83,334 a $208,333: 2.00% De $208,334 a $291,666: 2.50% No es tasa marginal. Todo tu ingreso del mes paga la misma tasa. Sin sorpresas. Ejemplo: si facturaste $40,000 en marzo, tu ISR es $440. Listo. El ahorro real en pesos Comparamos cuánto paga un contribuyente en RESICO contra el régimen general: Ingreso $25,000: ISR RESICO $250 vs Reg. General ~$3,500. Te ahorras $3,250/mes. Ingreso $45,000: ISR RESICO $495 vs Reg. General ~$7,000. Te ahorras $6,505/mes. Ingreso $80,000: ISR RESICO $1,200 vs Reg. General ~$16,000. Te ahorras $14,800/mes. Ingreso $150,000: ISR RESICO $3,000 vs Reg. General ~$36,000. Te ahorras $33,000/mes. Ahorro anual promedio: $78,060. Eso son $6,505 que te quedas cada mes. Tus obligaciones mes a mes Declaración de ISR. Presenta tu pago provisional de ISR antes del día 17 del mes siguiente. Declaración de IVA. Presenta tu declaración mensual de IVA en el mismo plazo: día 17. Emitir facturas CFDI. Por cada ingreso que recibas, sin excepción. Incluyendo cobros en efectivo. Declarar en ceros. Si no tuviste ingresos en el mes, presenta la declaración de todas formas. Desde 2026, RESICO ya no presenta declaración anual. Tus pagos mensuales son definitivos. IVA en RESICO: la confusión más común RESICO simplifica el ISR, pero el IVA funciona igual que en cualquier otro régimen. Cobras 16% de IVA a tus clientes, lo desglosas en tu factura, presentas declaración mensual de IVA y puedes acreditar el IVA que pagaste en tus compras. Si le facturas a una empresa (persona moral), te retienen 1.25% de ISR y 10.67% de IVA sobre el subtotal. Esas retenciones las descuentas en tu declaración. 5 errores que te sacan de RESICO No presentar 2 declaraciones seguidas. Dos meses consecutivos sin declarar y el SAT te cambia al régimen general sin aviso. No tener la e.firma vigente. Desde enero 2026 es obligatoria. Si venció y no la renovaste, estás en riesgo. Buzón tributario inactivo. Sin buzón verificado pueden restringirte los sellos. Sin sellos, no puedes facturar. Ser socio de una persona moral sin saberlo. Si te dieron de alta como socio de una empresa, aunque no participes, el SAT lo detecta. No facturar todos tus ingresos. El SAT cruza info bancaria con CFDI. Discrepancias entre depósitos y facturas = alerta. La consecuencia: te mandan al régimen general con tasas hasta 35%. Una vez fuera por incumplimiento, no regresas. RESICO vs Actividad Empresarial RESICO: Tasa ISR 1% a 2.5% sobre ingresos | Sin deducciones | Límite $3.5M/año | Contabilidad simplificada | Sin declaración anual | Ideal para margen alto, pocos gastos Act. Empresarial: Tasa ISR 1.92% a 35% sobre utilidad | Sí deducciones | Sin límite | Contabilidad electrónica completa | Declaración anual obligatoria | Ideal para margen bajo, muchos gastos La regla rápida: Si tus gastos deducibles son menos del 60-70% de tus ingresos, RESICO te conviene. Si tienes muchos gastos (comercio con inventario, manufactura, nómina), Actividad Empresarial puede salir mejor porque pagas ISR sobre la utilidad real. Ejemplo real: Mariana, diseñadora freelance Mariana trabaja desde casa, tiene 4 clientes fijos y factura $45,000 al mes. Sus gastos son mínimos: internet, Adobe y café. ISR anual en RESICO: $5,940. Ahorro anual vs régimen general: $66,060.

title: Construction Partners, Inc. Announces Fiscal 2026 Third Quarter Results
summary: Revenue Up 28% Compared to Q3 FY25 Adjusted Net Income Up 34% Compared to Q3 FY25 Adjusted EBITDA Up 24% Compared to Q3 FY25 Record Backlog of…...
body_text: Revenue Up 28% Compared to Q3 FY25 Adjusted Net Income Up 34% Compared to Q3 FY25 Adjusted EBITDA Up 24% Compared to Q3 FY25 Record Backlog of $3.36 Billion Company Raises FY26 Outlook DOTHAN, Ala. , Aug. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Construction Partners, Inc. (NASDAQ: ROAD) ("CPI" or the "Company"), a vertically integrated civil infrastructure company specializing in the construction and maintenance of roadways in local markets throughout the Sunbelt, today reported financial and operating results for the fiscal third quarter ended June 30, 2026. Fred J. (Jule) Smith, III, the Company's President and Chief Executive Officer, said, "Our strong third quarter results reflect the continued execution of our operating strategy and the dedication of our teams throughout the CPI family of companies. During the quarter, we delivered revenue growth of 28% and Adjusted EBITDA growth of 24%, despite the impact of energy cost inflation and extremely wet weather in May across many of our markets. These results underscore the resilience of our decentralized operating model, the strength of our local market strategy, and our ability to consistently execute across diverse market conditions. Demand for both public infrastructure and commercial construction projects remained healthy throughout our markets, driving backlog to a record $3.36 billion and providing continued visibility into future growth." Revenues were $999.4 million in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, an increase of 28.2% compared to $779.3 million in the same quarter last year. Gross profit was $168.4 million in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, compared to $131.8 million in the same quarter last year. General and administrative expenses were $63.1 million in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, compared to $51.0 million in the same quarter last year, and as a percentage of total revenues, decreased 20 basis points to 6.3%, compared to 6.5% in the same quarter last year. Net income was $59.6 million in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, compared to net income of $44.0 million in the same quarter last year. Adjusted net income(1) was $60.6 million in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, compared to Adjusted net income of $45.2 million in the same quarter last year. Using Adjusted net income, diluted earnings per share would have been $1.08 for the third quarter of fiscal 2026, compared to $0.81 in the same quarter last year. Adjusted EBITDA(1) in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 was $163.0 million, an increase of 23.8% compared to $131.7 million in the same quarter last year. Project backlog was a record $3.36 billion at June 30, 2026, compared to $2.94 billion at June 30, 2025 and $3.14 billion at March 31, 2026. Smith added, "Earlier this month, we were pleased to expand our Oklahoma footprint through the acquisition of Ellsworth Construction, which further strengthens our presence into two of the fastest-growing markets in the Sunbelt. Ellsworth adds experienced employees, strategically located facilities, and a strong reputation for execution, enhancing our ability to serve the rapidly growing Tulsa and Oklahoma City metropolitan areas. The acquisition also expands our capabilities in the fast-growing data center construction market, where Ellsworth has established a strong presence that complements Overland's extensive data center portfolio in North Texas. Based on our strong third quarter performance and the expected contribution from Ellsworth, we are raising our fiscal 2026 guidance. We remain on track to deliver sustained revenue growth, expanding profitability, and continued progress toward achieving our ROAD 2030 objectives." Fiscal 2026 Outlook The Company is raising its outlook for fiscal year 2026 with regard to revenue, net income, Adjusted net income, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA margin as follows: Revenue in the range of $3.640 billion to $3.680 billion Net income in the range of $165.0 million to $168.0 million Adjusted net income(1) in the range $177.6 million to $181.4 million Adjusted EBITDA(1) in the range of $559.0 million to $569.0 million Adjusted EBITDA margin(1) in the range of 15.36% to 15.46% Ned N. Fleming, III, the Company's Executive Chairman, stated, "CPI continues to create long-term shareholder value through the disciplined execution of our proven growth strategy, combining strong organic growth with strategic acquisitions that expand our platforms across the Sunbelt, increase scale, and enhance operating efficiencies. Supported by a strong balance sheet, experienced leadership team, and healthy customer funding for both public and private construction projects, we believe CPI is well positioned to continue growing and compounding value. The Board and I remain highly confident in CPI's long-term strategy, competitive position, and our ability to capitalize on the significant opportunities ahead." Conference Call The Company will conduct a conference call today at 10:00 a.m. Eastern Time (9:00 a.m. Central Time) to discuss financial and operating results for the fiscal quarter ended June 30, 2026. To access the call live by phone, dial (412) 902-0003 and ask for the Construction Partners call at least 10 minutes prior to the start time. A webcast of the call will also be available live and for later replay on the Company's Investor Relations website at www.constructionpartners.net . About Construction Partners, Inc. Construction Partners, Inc. is a vertically integrated civil infrastructure company operating in local markets throughout the Sunbelt in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas. Supported by its hot-mix asphalt plants, aggregate facilities and liquid asphalt terminals, the Company focuses on the construction, repair and maintenance of surface infrastructure. Publicly funded projects make up the majority of its business and include local and state roadways, interstate highways, airport runways and bridges. The company also performs private sector projects that include paving and sitework for office and industrial parks, shopping centers, local businesses and residential developments. To learn more, visit www.constructionpartners.net .
