title: Catering & Commissary: The New Back-of-House Growth Engine
summary: Catering and commissary kitchens are becoming real growth channels across foodservice. Here's why the back-of-house — not the order screen — decides who scales.
body_text: Can your back-of-house scale catering and commissary orders without adding another system? For a long time, catering was something a lot of operators did on the side. A few trays for lunch at the office down the street, an order for graduation parties in June. Nice to have, but not exactly a growth engine. That's changed. Catering, commissary production, and grab-and-go have quietly become some of the most lucrative growth channels in foodservice — and the operators who treat them that way are pulling ahead. Recent trade reporting from Nation’s Restaurant News shows catering emerging as a genuine revenue engine for some of the country's largest chains, with catering average unit volumes running several times higher than a typical mealtime transaction. Workplace demand is holding, too: catering research covered by Food On Demand found that 91% of workplaces plan to spend the same or more on food this year – up from 82% in 2024–and one in five plan to bump their food spending by more than 25%. Here's the part that doesn't make the headlines. The technology most operators bought to chase that growth was built for the front of house — taking orders and routing them. Saying yes to that demand is exactly the right call and is how a counter quietly grows into a real program. But an order booked isn’t an order fulfilled, and the setup behind the counter was never built to scale production, food safety, and labeling all at once. Nail those three and the catering program starts to compound on itself; leave them running on memory and sticky notes, and it buckles under its own success. Why catering exposes a back-of-house problem When a catering order comes in, the hard part isn't accepting orders. It's filling those orders safely, labeling them correctly, and getting them out the door without an allergen error or a missing date code — at a volume the kitchen wasn't staffed for on an ordinary Tuesday. So what now? Many operators need a quick solution and start bolting things on. A standalone system for specialty catering labels. A manual workaround for large-batch prep. Extra staff hours spent on tasks crutching up a process a single-transaction system was never designed to handle. Every one of those additions is another line item eating into the margin catering was supposed to create. You grow the top line and quietly give it back on the bottom. The blind spot isn't the ordering technology. It's that the ordering technology only solves half of the equation needed for a successful catering program. Why catering growth needs BOHA! by TransAct behind the counter I'll be direct about our point of view, because it's the whole reason we built the platform the way we did. BOHA! doesn't ask operators to add another system to manage growth. The same infrastructure that runs food safety and labeling in-store today — BOHA! Labeling, Food Prep, Temp, Sense, Checklist, all feeding the Control Center — extends to catering, commissary, and grab-and-go without new hardware, new software, or new headcount just to keep pace with demand. An operator already running BOHA! in-store can simply start fulfilling on catering and commissary orders using the same platform. No new systems to buy, no new tools for the team to learn, and no gap in food safety coverage as the business grows. That matters because of what information is needed to support catering orders to ensure they are safe to consume: allergens, prep-and-expiration tracking, nutritional and health-code labeling, MRD (Made, Ready, Discard) tracking, employee initials, prep timestamps. The same standards that apply to a single grab-and-go sandwich apply automatically to a 300-person order — whether one location's staff handles it or a centralized commissary team serving many stores. The label on the tray carries the same rigor as the label on the sandwich because it comes from the same place. The practical version: the same platform that labels a single grab-and-go item today can label a 200-person catering order tomorrow, without bolting on a separate system or retraining the team from scratch. Not sure what belongs on every catering, tray, and grab-and-go label ? Use our free checklist to review the key labeling elements operators need to manage across channels—from allergens and date codes to prep details and location information. Download the Catering & Commissary Labeling Checklist → Our perspective: this isn't just a restaurant story Here's what I think gets missed in the catering conversation. It gets framed as a restaurant-and-c-store story, because that's where the headlines are. But the capability — connected production, labeling, and food-safety documentation that scales into off-premise and centralized-kitchen workflows — applies just as directly to several other corners of foodservice that are growing the exact same way. Convenience stores and QSRs. This is the visible, leading edge of the trend. Grab-and-go programs expand into catering and commissary supply; a single platform means the labeling and food-safety standards that already run the store extend to the new channel instead of fragmenting across new tools. Sushi and other contract foodservice programs. A high-volume sushi program is a catering-and-commissary operation whether anyone calls it that or not — centralized prep, made-to-order and pre-packaged items, allergen-sensitive labeling, short shelf lives, and distribution across many locations. The same on-demand, FDA-compliant labeling and prep tracking that keep a multi-location sushi program consistent are exactly what a catering expansion needs. It’s the same reason contract sushi programs can hold labeling standards across thousands of locations. Foodservice management (FSM) companies. Contract foodservice operators running dining for hospitals, campuses, and corporate accounts live and die on standardization across sites they don't fully own. Catering and commissary production are core to that business, not an add-on — and every client account brings its own compliance and reporting requirements. A connected platform is how you hold one food-safety standard across all of it and prove it to each client, from a single lunch order to a year-end graduation party order for hundreds. Casino food and beverage . Casinos run some of the largest banquet, buffet, and catering operations in hospitality — high volume, high visibility events around the clock. That's a commissary-and-catering challenge at scale, with the same need for allergen accuracy, tray and buffet identification, and prep accountability. It's also where the foodservice side of our business and the gaming side of TransAct increasingly meet: the same operator modernizing the casino floor is modernizing the kitchens that feed it. The back-of-house rigor that runs a QSR's catering program runs a casino's banquet operation just as well. Different segments, same underlying shift: the kitchen behind the counter is becoming a revenue center, and the operators who win are the ones whose back-of-house can scale into it without turning into a patchwork of different systems. The bottom line Growth into catering and off-premise channels shouldn't require a technology overhaul. If the plan for scaling is "buy another system and hope it talks to the others," the margin the new channel creates is already leaking out through integration seams and retraining time. The operators pulling ahead aren't the ones with the most tools. They're the ones running the fewest — one platform that already knows how to keep food safe, label it accurately, and prove it did both, wherever that food is going. Catering, commissary, grab-and-go, banquet. Same standard. Same system. That's the whole idea. This perspective follows our latest announcement on the expanded catering and commissary capabilities in the BOHA! platform. To see exactly what's now supported — from large-batch production and centralized commissary workflows to catering labels, allergen and nutrition labeling, and "Made At / Distributed To" location labeling — read the full announcement here. Frequently asked questions What's the difference between a catering kitchen and a commissary kitchen? A catering kitchen produces food for off-site events and orders. A commissary (or central) kitchen produces food centrally for distribution to multiple locations. Many operators run both, and the same production, labeling, and food-safety workflows apply to each. Why does catering create food-safety risk? Volume and distance. High-volume production increases the chance of an allergen or date-code error, and off-premise food is held and transported longer — so labeling accuracy and prep-and-expiration tracking matter more, not less. Do you need separate software for catering labels? Not if your in-store labeling platform already scales. Running separate systems for in-store, catering, and grab-and-go labels adds cost and integration risk; a connected platform prints all of them from the same place. Does this apply outside restaurants? Yes. Convenience stores, sushi and contract foodservice programs, foodservice management companies, and casino banquet operations all run catering or commissary production and face the same back-of-house scaling challenge.

body_text: We pointed Cascade , Escape's AI pentesting engine , at a production AI agent that a large organization runs internally. The agent had a guardrail built to catch prompt injection . Cascade got past it on the second try. The trick wasn't a smarter payload, just a different pretext, and the agent handed over its entire system prompt : the tools it could call, the rules it followed, and the session details attached to the conversation. That alone gives an attacker what they need to go straight at the agent's tools instead of guessing at them blind. The target The target was an internal AI assistant. Authenticated employees could ask it questions about documents they'd uploaded, and it answered using a mix of retrieval and tool calls. Like most agents shipped this way, it had a guardrail sitting between the user and the model, there to catch prompt injection before it reached the model. The bypass Severity: high (full system prompt and tool metadata disclosure). Requires an authenticated session. The guardrail stopped Cascade exactly once. Cascade's first move was the obvious one, the move every guardrail is built for: ask directly for the system prompt. That got blocked and logged, exactly as designed. The second message wasn't a stronger version of the first. It was a different request. Cascade wrapped the same ask in a context the agent had no reason to distrust, something closer to a research or documentation request, phrased the way a colleague or an academic would phrase it. Nothing about it read as an attack. The agent obliged. Several thousand characters came back: the full list of tools it could reach, the rules for when it was allowed to call each one, the exact citation format it used, and the session identifiers tied to the conversation. It handed all of that over because the request sounded reasonable, not because a technical control broke. That last point is the one worth dwelling on. The guardrail wasn't beaten by a cleverer string, it was talked out of doing its job, the same way a good pretext gets a helpful employee to read a password over the phone. Cascade didn't find a vulnerability in the code. It found the sentence that made the agent want to help. No human wrote that sentence. Cascade did, after reading the refusal it got the first time. Reproducing the bypass The screenshots below are a reproduction. The engagement is under NDA, so we rebuilt the setup in a lab: same guardrail behavior as the assessment, a synthetic system prompt of comparable length and structure, and a reworded injection. Cascade treated the refusal as information rather than a dead end. It kept the objective and changed the register in a new chat. Synthetic system prompt returned in full The whole thing came back at once, around 8,200 characters in the real engagement. Knowledge cutoff, tool-calling protocol, the full tool list, the citation format, the session identifier. What the leak opens up A system prompt is the rulebook an attacker would otherwise have to reconstruct one blocked request at a time. With the tool list and the constraints in hand, there's no more guessing about which tools exist or what sets them off - an attacker can go straight at the ones worth targeting. The session details that came with it push things further still, toward tracking or replaying a specific conversation. What this says about AI pentesting and the state of security in the next few years The bypass itself isn't the interesting part. Getting a guardrail to reconsider a blocked request by changing the framing is a known move. What's newer is how building that bypass looked from the inside: no wordlist, no brute force, just one AI system reading how another one reasons and finding the angle nobody had told it to watch. That's the shift worth naming. Defensive agents are built to reason about intent rather than match strings, so testing them credibly now takes an attacker that reasons too, one that treats a rejection as information rather than a dead end. A scanner with a fixed payload list gets a single shot, the one that gets logged and blocked. Cascade got a second shot because it understood why the first one failed. Throwing known jailbreaks at a chatbot doesn't really describe AI security testing anymore. What's happening now looks more like two reasoning systems working against each other in real time, one holding a line and one probing for where the line actually gives. That isn't a future scenario. It's an ordinary engagement today, and it's where offensive security is headed. Fixing it The fix isn't a better keyword list. A few things help more. Semantic input classification looks at what a request is trying to do rather than the specific words it uses. Output-side filtering blocks system-prompt and configuration disclosure regardless of how the request got there, so it catches the cases the input side misses. Least-privilege prompting keeps anything out of the system prompt that would seriously help an attacker if it leaked, on the assumption that something eventually will. And re-testing has to be continuous, because a guardrail that holds today against known phrasing tells you nothing about whether it holds against a reframing no one has tried yet (or a smarter AI model). Conclusion Two things happened in this engagement: a production agent gave up its full configuration, and it did so to another AI that just asked better. Fixing that doesn't take new tooling on the target's side. Catching it does take testing at the same cadence, and with the same kind of reasoning, as the thing trying to get in. If your security program tests AI agents the way it tests everything else, once a year against a snapshot, it's worth asking what has already slipped past that filter in the months since. title: How to Build Passwordless Auth Using TOTP With Twilio Verify in PHP
summary: In this tutorial, you will learn how to implement TOTP-based passwordless authentication in PHP using Twilio Verify.
body_text:
Time to read: August 10, 2026 Written by Matthew Setter Twilion AI generated summary Deploy passwordless authentication using TOTP with Twilio Verify. This enhances security and user experience by eliminating passwords. Building the app involves QR code scanning, creating factors, and validating TOTP codes. This summary was generated by AI and reviewed by the Twilio team. How to Build Passwordless Auth Using TOTP With Twilio Verify in PHP Typing or generating a unique password for every new account or website is a hassle. Although password managers help, passwordless auth (authentication) offers a more streamlined and secure alternative. In this tutorial, you will learn about passwordless auth, and build a PHP app that uses Twilio Verify to implement it. Programming language support You can find this tutorial in the following programming languages: Go Prerequisites Before you begin, ensure you have the following: A free Twilio account. Click here to create a free account if you are new to Twilio. An authentication app, such as Twilio Authy PHP (ideally, version 8.5) Your favourite text editor or IDE (such as neovim or Visual Studio Code) Your favourite web browser Architecture This application will be a simplistic web-based application, split up over three stages. Stage one: the user will submit their username to begin setting up Two-factor Authentication (2FA). Stage two: they'll set up a TOTP entry in their authenticator app. They'll do this with their authenticator app by scanning a QR code or entering a unique code. Then, they'll submit the initial code that their authenticator app generates for them. If the code is valid, their account is ready to use. Stage three:, They can validate future codes which their authenticator app generates for them in the final form in the application. What is passwordless auth? Passwordless auth is an authentication method where the user does not need a password in order to log into an app or system. Rather, the user's mobile device receives a one-time code. In this authentication method, users are authenticated using other unique and more secure alternatives like Time-based One-time Passwords (TOTP, or Soft Token) , SMS, Passkeys , Silent Network Authentication (SNA), Voice , or email notification . Here's a breakdown of how it works, using TOTP: User initiation: When a user creates an account, instead of entering a password, they create a new Factor resource with Twilio Verify — initially marked as unverified — seeding it with a unique (auto-generated) identifier. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app: Using an authenticator app such as Twilio Authy , they scan the QR code then enter the code that the authenticator app provides. The code is validated using Twilio Verify. If the code is valid the Factor is marked verified. The authenticator app can now provide time-based codes to use in the future, when logging in, which Twilio Verify will verify. Code validation: When the user logs in, they enter their username and a TOTP code generated by their authenticator app. The application then uses Twilio Verify to validate the code along with their unique identifier. This approach significantly enhances security by leveraging the inherent security features of the user's mobile device as a second factor in the authentication process. It also eliminates the need for them to memorize passwords, thereby simplifying the authentication process and enhancing user convenience. Passwordless authentication has additional advantages, including the following: Enhanced security: Reduces the risk of password-related breaches. Convenience: Eliminates the need for users to remember and manage multiple passwords. Reduced friction: Streamlines the login process, improving the user experience. Scalability: Easily scalable with Twilio's infrastructure. Build the app Step 1: Set up the project Set up a new project using the Twilio / Slim Base Project , by running the following command, where you store your PHP projects: Copy code composer create-project settermjd/twilio-slim-base-project twilio-verify-totp-php cd twilio-verify-totp-php mkdir -p templates public/css Step 2: Install the required dependencies Next, install the required dependencies, by running the following: Copy code composer require bryanjhv/slim-session chillerlan/php-qrcode slim/flash slim/twig-view twilio/sdk vlucas/phpdotenv In case you're not familiar with them, here's a short description of the dependencies that you just installed: chillerlan PHP-QRCode : This simplifies generating QR codes in the application PHP dotenv : Loads environment variables from .env into getenv() , $_ENV and $_SERVER automagically. Slim Flash : This adds flash message support, which simplifies providing UI feedback throughout the application Slim Session : Simple middleware for Slim Framework 4, that allows managing PHP built-in sessions Slim Framework Twig View : This is a Slim Framework view helper built on top of the Twig templating component. Twilio's PHP Helper Library : This simplifies integrating with Twilio in PHP Now, open the project directory in your preferred text editor or IDE. Step 3: Set the required environment variables Dotenv files (commonly named .env ) are used to store the configuration information that your app needs during development, separate from the application's code. For this tutorial, it will be your Twilio credentials (i.e., your Twilio Account SID and Auth Token) and a Verify Service SID . In your project's top-level directory, open .env and add the following variable to the end of the file; the other two variables have already been set in the file. Copy code TWILIO_VERIFY_SERVICE_SID= You next need to retrieve the credentials to set as their values. To do that, sign into the Twilio Console . There, click the black and white up arrow at the bottom of the page, and you should see your Account SID and Auth Token in the Workbench ; as shown in the image below. Copy these values and paste them into .env as the values for TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID and TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN . Next, navigate to Products and Services > Verify > Services . On this page, click Create new . Then, fill out the initial form with the configuration values shown in the screenshot below, and click Continue . In the next step, leave Enable Fraud Guard set to "Yes" and click Continue to finish creating the service. The factor is seeded by a string created with random_bytes . This is then converted to hex format, of which the first 32 characters are retrieved, keeping it within the 8 - 64 character limit . As this is required later in the application, it's then stored in the current session. Following this, it's used to create a new factor resource using the Twilio Rest Client. From the response to that request the following properties are stored in session for later use, the: Friendly Name: The Factor's friendly name SID: A 34 character string that uniquely identifies the Factor. URL: The URL of the Factor resource. Then, if the new Factor's status is set to "unverified", the user is redirected to the verify-totp route. The getNamedRoute() function is a small utility function for retrieving a route object from the application based on its name. These objects contain details about one of the application's routes. title: Figma Weave alternatives: 6 tools compared for 2026
summary: The best Figma Weave alternatives for 2026, from hands-on canvases (Krea, Flair, Recraft) to a briefed agent for product visuals.
body_text: TL;DR The best Figma Weave alternative depends on how you want to work: keep operating a canvas or node graph by hand, or brief an agent and let it produce. For a hands-on canvas, Krea AI is the closest rival; to produce on-brand product visuals at scale, Presti is the pick. Krea AI is best for creatives who want a real-time canvas with a node workflow builder and every frontier image and video model in one place. Flair AI is best for marketers who want to art-direct product scenes and ad creatives on a drag-and-drop canvas. Presti is best for retailers and brands, because you brief it in plain language and it produces on-brand product photos, 360° spins and video at catalog scale, with team review. Playground is best for social and design images, with a simple app and a generous free tier. Recraft is best for designers who need vectors, icons and on-style illustrations, not just raster images. Two ways to make AI visuals: operate a canvas, or brief an agent Node-based visual tools had a real moment. Weavy, Freepik and Flora, among others, pushed the same idea, and in late 2025 Figma acquired Weavy, reportedly for more than $200M, turning it into Figma Weave. It is a striking tool: a node-based canvas in the browser that routes each step to a fitting model and lets you branch, remix and refine with hands-on edits like masking, relighting and color grading. Figma calls the idea “generative craft,” and that phrase is the whole point: the canvas is for people who want to steer every step themselves. That is also the reason people look for an alternative. Operating a canvas or a node graph is powerful, but it is work: you place the nodes, pick the models, and drive each iteration. So the real question behind “Figma Weave alternatives” is not which tool has the most models. It is whether you want to keep operating the canvas, or hand the production to something that briefs like a teammate. This guide compares six tools along exactly that line. Five are canvas or node tools you drive by hand: Figma Weave itself, plus Krea AI, Flair AI, Playground and Recraft. One, Presti, takes the other approach: you describe the outcome, it asks questions, plans the work and produces in batch. Presti is our own product, so we hold its section to the same standard as the rest and are upfront about where a canvas is the better choice. How we compared these Figma Weave alternatives We did not run a scripted benchmark across all six tools, so this comparison includes no quality scores. Output quality depends heavily on the model you pick and the prompt you write, and most of these tools route to the same frontier models anyway, so a single score would mislead. Instead we compared them on the things that decide whether the tool fits how you work, all read from each vendor's own pages on 18 August 2026. How you work: do you operate a canvas or node graph by hand, or brief an agent that plans and produces? Outputs: images, video, vectors, 3D, and whether the tool is built for one-off craft or repeatable production. Model breadth: how many image and video models you can reach without juggling subscriptions. Brand consistency and review: can it hold one look across a catalog, and does it have team roles and sign-off? Real cost and rights: the monthly price and credits, and whether output is licensed for commercial use. One note on pricing. We quote standard monthly billing where a vendor publishes it; annual plans are usually cheaper. Where a tool meters credits, we say what the plan includes rather than invent a precise cost per image. Where a figure is not published clearly, we flag it. Figma Weave alternatives at a glance Figma Weave and five alternatives compared. Standard monthly billing, USD, verified 18 August 2026. Tool Type Best for Entry price (monthly) Free tier Watch-out Figma Weave Node-based AI media canvas Designers and VFX pros who want to craft each shot Starter $24 Yes (150 credits) Hands-on canvas; no API yet; credits meter every step Krea AI Real-time AI creative canvas + nodes Creatives wanting every model on one canvas Basic $9 Yes (100/day) Heavy video use burns credits fast Flair AI AI scene and product canvas Marketers art-directing product scenes and ads Pro $10 (license from $35) Yes (5 images) Product fidelity can distort fine text or reflective surfaces Playground AI image and design app Social and design images on a budget Pro $15 Yes Image only, no video; credit caps on top models Recraft AI design tool (vector + raster) Designers needing vectors, icons and on-style art Basic $12 Yes (no commercial) Design-focused; no video; free output is non-commercial Presti AI product photography agent Retailers and brands producing on-brand visuals at scale Pro from $49 Yes (60 credits) Built for product visuals and volume, not free-form art Pricing and free-tier details verified on 18 August 2026. Entry price is the cheapest paid plan. This category moves fast, so re-check each vendor's pricing page. Figma Weave: the tool you are comparing against Figma Weave is an AI-native media platform, built from the Weavy tool Figma acquired. You work on a node-based canvas: generate an image or a clip, then branch it, remix it and refine it with professional edits like object masking, relighting and color grading. It routes each node to a fitting model, naming Seedance, Sora and Veo for video and Flux, Ideogram, Nano-Banana and Seedream for images. It handles images, video, animation and visual effects, and it is aimed at people who want to push past the first prompt: designers, VFX artists, marketers and enterprise teams. Best for: designers, VFX artists and creative teams who want a hands-on node canvas to craft and refine each shot across many models. Where it falls short. The canvas is powerful but manual, so it rewards craft time rather than volume, and it is not built to keep a whole product catalog on-brand on its own. There is no public API yet (Enterprise only, coming), and because every step spends credits, heavy iteration adds up. Pricing. On standard monthly billing, Free gives 150 credits a month and up to 5 workflows, Starter is $24 (1,500 credits), Professional is $45 (4,000 credits) and Team is $60 per user (4,500 credits each), with Enterprise on a custom quote. Annual billing is roughly 20% cheaper. Unused credits roll over up to three months on Professional and Team, and top-ups run about $10 for 1,000 to 1,200 credits. Each model node shows its own credit cost, so budget by how much you iterate. The other canvas and node tools These four tools share Figma Weave's core idea: an interface you operate yourself, whether that is a real-time canvas, a node graph, or a design surface. They differ in focus, from every-model creative canvases to design-specific and product-specific ones. Krea AI: the closest all-model canvas Krea AI is the nearest like-for-like: a real-time creative canvas that also ships a node workflow builder, Krea Nodes, so you can chain steps much as you would in Weave. It leans on breadth, generating images, video, 3D and enhancements, and giving paid users the full roster of video models, naming Veo3, Sora and Kling alongside its own Krea models. Real-time generation and aggressive upscaling (up to 22K on higher tiers) are the draw for creatives who want to explore fast and keep everything in one place. Best for: creatives and studios who want a fast, hands-on canvas with a node builder and every frontier image and video model under one subscription. Where it falls short. It is still a tool you operate, so it does not keep a catalog on-brand for you, and heavy video use runs through credits quickly. It is built for creative exploration rather than catalog-wide production. Pricing. A free plan gives about 100 units a day. On standard monthly billing, Basic is $9 (5,000 units), Pro is $35 (20,000 units) and Max is $105 (60,000 units), with Business and Enterprise above; annual billing saves about 40%. A commercial license and Krea Nodes are included from the Basic plan up. Flair AI: art-direct product scenes on a canvas Flair AI is a drag-and-drop scene canvas aimed at commerce and marketing. You place your product alongside props and 3D assets, set the lighting and camera, then generate, so you art-direct the shot rather than describe it in one prompt. It adds AI fashion models, virtual try-on, upscaling, variations, short product videos, bulk generation and templates, with API access on higher tiers. It is a natural pick if you want visual control over each scene and a steady stream of ad and social variations. Best for: marketers, designers and agencies who want to compose product scenes and ad creatives on a canvas. Where it falls short. In our experience, product fidelity can be a weak point, with fine text and reflective surfaces more prone to distortion, so test your hardest product first. A commercial license only unlocks from the Pro+ plan up, and image allowances per tier are modest for true catalog volume. Pricing. The free plan gives 5 generated images and 1 video, with no commercial license. Pro is $10 a month, Pro+ is $35 a month (80 images, company commercial license), and Scale starts at $55 a month (150 images), scaling up on a slider, with Enterprise custom. Commercial rights begin at Pro+, so the real entry point for business use is $35. The prices are shown in dollars but the page does not label the currency, so confirm it. Playground: simple image and design app Playground is a lighter, image-first app for social posts and design graphics. You work on a simple canvas, generate with a few frontier models, and get design helpers like templates, upscaling, background removal and AI-extend. It is not a node tool and it does not do video, but it is easy to pick up and has a generous free tier, which makes it a good fit when you mostly need still images and quick design assets rather than a full craft pipeline. Best for: social and marketing teams who want quick, affordable still images and simple design tools, with a worldwide royalty-free license. Where it falls short. It is image only, with no video and no node graph, and access to the top models is capped by monthly credits, so it is lighter than Weave or Krea for serious craft or motion. Pricing. The free plan creates up to 10 images every 3 hours with a small monthly allowance across Nano Banana, GPT Image 2 and Seedream. Pro is $15 a month (up to 75 images every 3 hours and 150 monthly credits across those models), and Pro Plus is $45 a month (unlimited image generations, 1,000 monthly credits across all models, higher resolution and API eligibility). All plans carry a worldwide royalty-free license. Recraft: design, vectors and on-style art Recraft is the design specialist of the group. Beyond raster images, it generates true vector art, icons, 3D-style images and illustrations, and it lets you lock a consistent style across a set, which designers value for brand systems, websites and print. It works on a design canvas rather than a node graph, and it is the only tool here built around vector output, so it fills a gap the others leave open. Best for: designers and brand teams who need vectors, icons and on-style illustrations, not just photographic images. Where it falls short. It is focused on design and illustration, with no video, and its free plan grants no commercial rights (free output is public and owned by Recraft), so you need a paid plan to use anything commercially. It is not built for product photography or catalog production. Pricing. The free plan gives 50 credits a day but no commercial use. Basic is $12 a month for 1,000 credits, and the Pro tiers scale by resolution at $20 (2K), $40 (4K) and $80 (8K) a month, with one credit per raster image and two per vector. All paid plans grant full ownership and commercial rights. Subscription credits reset monthly and do not roll over, though top-ups do not expire. A different approach: an agent, not a canvas The five tools above all put you at the controls. The alternative is to stop operating the interface and start briefing it. That is the shift Presti makes, and it matters most when the goal is not one crafted hero shot but many on-brand visuals across a catalog. We did not reach this view from the outside. In February 2026 we shipped a node-based version of Presti, built on the same premise as the tools above: wire the workflow once, run it on hundreds of products. It worked when everything went to plan, and got painful the moment reality turned messy. A missing node became a blocker, an edge case broke the flow, a new input format created friction, and real inputs like PDFs and untidy CSVs were awkward to handle. Every fix made the platform heavier: more nodes, more parameters, more branching, until it was fine for a few power users and too much for everyone else. That is why we rebuilt Presti around an agent you brief rather than a graph you wire. Presti: brief an agent instead of driving a canvas Full disclosure: Presti is our own tool. We hold this section to the same factual standard as the others and are upfront about where a canvas is the better choice. Presti is our AI visual production platform for product photography and video. Instead of a canvas you operate, it works like a teammate you brief: you describe the outcome and attach your product photo, the agent asks clarifying questions, plans the production and generates in batch. It produces packshots, lifestyle staging, 360° spins, product swaps and image-to-video, and a Brand Skill encodes your visual identity once so a large catalog stays on-brand. Like Weave and Krea, it routes each task to a fitting model rather than locking you to one, and it wraps everything in a team workspace with roles, in-context comments and approvals. It exports up to 4K, with upscaling to 8K and video to 1080p. ‍ Best for: retailers, marketplaces and brands that need on-brand product photos, 360° spins and video at catalog scale, with team review built in. Where it falls short. If you want to art-direct a single image pixel by pixel, or explore free-form creative and motion work, a hands-on canvas like Figma Weave or Krea gives you more direct control. Presti is built for on-brand product visuals and volume, not open-ended craft, and very complex or reflective products can still need a second pass. Pricing. A free plan gives 60 credits a month, about 20 images or 2 videos. Pro starts at $49 a month for 500 credits, about 166 images or 16 videos, with a selectable higher volume, credit rollover, on-demand top-ups and unlimited content storage shared across unlimited users. An image is 3 credits and a video 30, so on Pro that is about $0.30 an image or $3 a video. title: Biosimilars for Humira: An IBD Patient Guide
summary: Compare Humira biosimilars, devices, coverage, and switching rules.
body_text: The FDA product list shows that Humira has more U.S. biosimilars than any other inflammatory bowel disease biologic. That gives insurers and patients more options, while the names, devices, concentrations, and coverage rules can be difficult to sort out. Every FDA-approved adalimumab biosimilar must be highly similar to Humira and have no clinically meaningful difference in safety or effectiveness. The FDA's patient guide says biosimilars provide the same treatment benefits, strength, dosage, and potential side effects as the reference product. The product your plan prefers can still change how a prescription is filled, how an injection feels, and what you pay. The U.S. Humira biosimilar list As of August 2026, the FDA biosimilar product list includes ten adalimumab products referencing Humira: Amjevita, Cyltezo, Hyrimoz, Hadlima, Abrilada, Hulio, Yusimry, Idacio, Yuflyma, and Simlandi. Their FDA applicants are Amgen, Boehringer Ingelheim, Sandoz, Samsung Bioepis, Pfizer, Mylan or Viatris, Coherus, Fresenius Kabi, Celltrion, and Alvotech, respectively, according to the FDA Purple Book product records . Those products are not identical packages. The Purple Book shows different approved strengths and presentations, including prefilled syringes and autoinjectors. It also separates high-concentration and original-concentration presentations. A patient switching products should confirm the brand, nonproprietary suffix, strength, dose, device, and injection schedule on the new prescription. Availability also changes over time, so FDA approval should not be treated as proof that a particular specialty pharmacy currently stocks every presentation. Which Humira biosimilars are interchangeable? Interchangeability is a regulatory designation related to pharmacy substitution. It gives no product a safety or effectiveness ranking. FDA states that both categories meet the same standards for quality and clinical similarity. An interchangeable biosimilar may be substituted for Humira without contacting the prescriber when state law permits it, while a non-interchangeable biosimilar can still be prescribed directly. The FDA review and approval guidance explains both points. The current Purple Book lists interchangeable presentations for Abrilada, Amjevita, Cyltezo, Hadlima, Hulio, Hyrimoz, Simlandi, and Yuflyma. It lists Idacio and Yusimry as biosimilars without that designation. Because interchangeability can be added through later FDA action and may apply to particular presentations, verify the exact product in the live Purple Book adalimumab results , which captures regulatory updates. What research says about switching Switching keeps the active treatment molecule within the adalimumab family. In the ADA-SWITCH study of 524 patients with IBD , switching from originator adalimumab to a biosimilar was not associated with more discontinuation, relapse, or adverse events than continuing the originator. That evidence supports clinical continuity for many patients, while individual symptoms and device experiences still deserve attention. Adalimumab products retain the class warnings and monitoring requirements of the reference drug. A new injector can also differ in grip, activation, needle visibility, or injection volume. Ask the specialty pharmacy for training if the device has changed. Record the first several doses, any injection reaction, missed or delayed doses, and changes in bowel symptoms. Report a suspected adverse effect or loss of disease control to the prescribing team before changing the dose or schedule. The first shipment deserves an extra check. Compare the medication label with the prescription, confirm that the quantity covers the full dosing period, and inspect the package for the correct storage instructions and expiration date. Arrange the refill before the final dose on hand, especially when a new authorization is still pending. If the new device feels unfamiliar, request manufacturer instructions or pharmacist-led training and perform the first injection only after the technique is clear. Insurance and out-of-pocket implications Self-injected adalimumab is often managed through a plan's pharmacy benefit and designated specialty pharmacy, while the controlling benefit and dispensing channel should be confirmed with the plan. An insurer may prefer one biosimilar, require a new prior authorization, or stop covering Humira. The Crohn's & Colitis Foundation recommends asking when a coverage change begins, what the new treatment will cost, whether copay assistance is available, and whether an appeal is appropriate. Out-of-pocket spending can remain high when a biosimilar has a lower list price. Deductibles, coinsurance, copay assistance rules, and the plan's negotiated terms can change the result. FDA specifically notes that reimbursement sits outside its role and advises patients to check coverage with their insurer. Before agreeing to a fill, request the exact copay, confirm whether assistance counts toward the deductible, and check that both the prescriber and specialty pharmacy have the correct product. Keeping the authorization letter, shipment dates, injection log, and pre-switch symptom baseline together makes a coverage disruption or clinical concern easier to document. title: Digital vs Traditional Background Verification in India: Why Companies Are Switching to Instant API Based Checks

body_text: Insights & Resources Digital vs Traditional Background Verification in India: Why Companies Are Switching to Instant API Based Checks August 7, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet In the early 2000s, verifying a single employee in India took an average of 15 to 21 days. A company would send the candidate’s documents to a verification agency. The agency would dispatch a field agent to the candidate’s home address for physical verification. Another team would call previous employers to confirm employment dates. Someone would visit the candidate’s college to verify their degree. And then the agency would compile everything into a PDF report and email it three weeks later. By the time that report arrived, one of three things had usually happened. The candidate had already joined another company that did not verify. The hiring manager had given up waiting and let the candidate start without verification. Or the candidate was sitting at home, losing income during the verification period, growing frustrated with a process they had no visibility into. This was the standard for two decades. And for two decades, it was good enough because there was no alternative. That era is over. Digital background verification, powered by API integrations with government databases, has compressed verification timelines from weeks to minutes. A PAN card that took a field agent three days to verify through paper based processes can now be checked against the Income Tax Department database in seconds. A Voter ID that required a physical visit to confirm can be validated against the Election Commission database instantly. An employment history that took two weeks of phone calls to previous employers can be cross referenced against EPFO records in minutes. This guide compares traditional and digital background verification across every dimension that matters to Indian businesses: speed, accuracy, cost, compliance, and scalability. If you are still using a traditional verification agency or a manual internal process, this will show you exactly what you are missing and why the switch is not just convenient but necessary. How Traditional Verification Works (And Why It Breaks Down) The Traditional Process In a traditional verification setup, the company collects document copies from the candidate and sends them to a verification agency. The agency assigns field agents for physical address verification and calls previous employers to confirm employment dates and designations. Education verification involves contacting universities or colleges, often through physical visits. Criminal record checks require court visits or engagement with local police. The agency compiles findings into a report after all checks are complete. Where It Fails Speed. The average turnaround for a traditional verification is 7 to 21 days. Some checks, particularly education verification and criminal record searches in courts that are not digitized, can take even longer. In a job market where top candidates receive multiple offers, three weeks of verification is three weeks of losing candidates to faster competitors. Accuracy. Traditional verification relies heavily on human judgment and manual processes. A field agent visiting an address might confirm the location exists without confirming the candidate actually lives there. A phone call to a previous employer might reach someone who gives inaccurate information. Human error in data recording, transcription, and report compilation introduces inaccuracies at every step. Fraud detection. Manual checks cannot detect sophisticated document forgery. A well made fake PAN card looks identical to a real one when examined by a field agent. Only an API based check against the actual Income Tax Department database can confirm whether the PAN number is valid and whether the name matches. Similarly, AI generated fake certificates and digitally altered documents are invisible to manual inspection but fail instantly when checked against source databases. Scalability. When a company needs to verify 50 candidates in a week during a growth phase, traditional agencies struggle. They do not have enough field agents. Phone lines are busy. University offices are closed during holidays. The process that works reasonably well for five candidates a month collapses when volume increases. Compliance. The DPDP Act 2023 requires that personal data be handled with consent, for a lawful purpose, and with appropriate safeguards. Traditional verification often involves photocopying documents, sharing them via email with multiple parties, storing them in physical files without access controls, and retaining them without clear policies. This casual handling of personal data is a compliance liability. Cost. Traditional verification agencies charge per check, per visit, and per report. A comprehensive verification involving address, education, employment, and criminal records can cost Rs 1,500 to Rs 5,000 per candidate. For a company hiring 100 people a year, this adds up to Rs 1.5 to 5 lakh annually just for verification. How Digital Verification Works Digital background verification uses API integrations with government and institutional databases to verify information at the source. Instead of sending a person to check if a PAN card is real, the platform sends the PAN number directly to the Income Tax Department’s database and gets an authoritative response in seconds. When multiple documents are verified, the platform runs cross record confidence analysis, automatically comparing details across all documents. Results arrive in minutes. No field agents. No phone calls. No waiting. They cannot check the PAN number against the central database. They might miss a subtle forgery. When an API checks a PAN number, it queries the Income Tax Department’s actual database. The response is authoritative. Either the PAN number exists and matches the claimed details, or it does not. There is no room for human judgment error, visual inspection failure, or subjective assessment. The answer comes directly from the source of truth. This distinction is particularly important now that AI generated forgeries have made visual document inspection unreliable. A fake PAN card created using modern design tools can fool any human inspector. It cannot fool an API check against the government database. Head to Head Comparison Speed Traditional: 7 to 21 days average turnaround. Some checks can take 30+ days. Digital: Minutes per check. A batch of 50 candidates can be verified in a single day. Accuracy Traditional: Dependent on field agent skill, honesty, and thoroughness. Subject to human error in recording and transcription. Cannot detect sophisticated document forgery. Digital: Database responses are authoritative. The Income Tax Department knows whether a PAN is valid. The Election Commission knows whether a Voter ID is genuine. The EPFO knows where PF contributions were made. No subjective assessment is involved. Cost Per Verification Traditional: Rs 500 to Rs 5,000 per candidate depending on the depth of checks. Additional charges for rush processing, re-verification, and physical visits to remote locations. Digital: A few rupees per check through platforms like ID Verify by SalaryBox. No per visit charges because there are no visits. No rush charges because every check is fast. The cost difference is dramatic, often 10x to 50x cheaper for identity verification checks. Geographic Coverage Traditional: Limited by the agency’s field agent network. Verifying a candidate from a remote district in Jharkhand requires finding a field agent who can travel there. Some agencies simply cannot cover certain areas. Digital: PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN databases are national. A candidate from any district in any state is verified against the same central database. There are no coverage gaps based on geography. Scalability Traditional: Linear scaling with headcount. Double the candidates, double the agents needed. Agencies often cannot handle sudden volume spikes, creating backlogs during peak hiring periods. Digital: Near infinite scalability. Whether you verify 5 candidates or 500, the platform processes each check in the same timeframe. No bottleneck from agent availability. Compliance Traditional: Paper based processes with multiple handoffs create DPDP Act compliance risks. Documents are photocopied, emailed, stored in physical files, and sometimes retained indefinitely without clear policies. Digital: Data flows through encrypted API connections. Document numbers are processed electronically without physical copies. Audit trails are automatic. Timestamped verification records are maintained digitally with proper access controls. With the DPDP Act now fully enforceable, the compliance advantage of digital verification is not just a preference. It is becoming a legal necessity. Fraud Detection Traditional: Relies on visual inspection and human judgment. Cannot detect AI generated document forgeries, digitally altered certificates, or sophisticated identity fraud. Digital: API based checks are immune to document forgery. A fake PAN card with a perfect visual appearance fails instantly when the number is checked against the government database. Cross record analysis automatically catches inconsistencies across multiple documents that a human reviewer might miss. The EPFO Data Masking Challenge One area where the shift to digital verification is not just advantageous but mandatory involves EPFO data. The 2025-26 EPFO data masking rules have changed how PF information is displayed on the EPFO portal. Previously, HR teams could manually log into the EPFO portal and view employee contribution details. Now, sensitive data is masked, making manual portal viewing insufficient for verification. Digital verification platforms with secure API integrations can retrieve source verified tenure data directly from the ECR system, bypassing the masking limitations. This means that the “old way” of manually checking the EPFO portal is no longer viable. Companies that have not switched to digital UAN verification are either getting incomplete data or violating data access protocols. Common Objections to Digital Verification (And Why They Do Not Hold Up) “Our traditional agency has served us well for years.” Your agency may have competent people, but they are fighting physics. They cannot make a field agent travel faster or a university respond sooner. The fundamental constraints of manual processes are speed and accuracy limitations that no amount of agency competence can overcome. “Digital verification does not cover everything we need.” This is partially valid. Some checks, like detailed reference interviews or in person address verification, benefit from human interaction. The solution is not to choose between digital and traditional. Use digital verification for identity, employment history, and document authentication, where databases provide authoritative answers. Use traditional methods for the remaining checks that genuinely require human interaction, like detailed reference conversations. “We are too small to need a verification platform.” Digital verification is actually more accessible for smaller companies than traditional agencies. Platforms like ID Verify by SalaryBox charge per check with no subscriptions, no minimum commitments, and no setup fees. A company with 10 employees can use it as easily as a company with 10,000. Most candidates prefer digital verification because it is faster, meaning they get their offer confirmed and their joining date set sooner. “We need physical address verification, which digital cannot provide.” For address verification specifically, physical visits may still add value. But consider that Voter ID verification through the Election Commission database provides the registered address associated with the Voter ID. This is a strong proxy for address confirmation that costs a fraction of a physical visit. How to Make the Switch Step 1: Audit Your Current Process Map your current verification process end to end. Step 5: Transition Remaining Checks After establishing digital verification for identity and employment, evaluate which remaining checks can also be digitized. Education verification is increasingly available through digital platforms. Criminal record searches through eCourts databases are faster than physical court visits. Keep traditional methods only for checks that genuinely require human interaction, such as detailed reference interviews or specialized investigations. Frequently Asked Questions Is digital verification legally valid in India? Yes. Digital verification checks document details against the same government databases that any official verification would use. The data returned by the Income Tax Department for a PAN check, the Election Commission for a Voter ID check, or the Ministry of Transport for a Driving Licence check is the same authoritative data that any court or regulator would rely on. body_text: That dashboard should be a skill Refactor complex dashboards into skills. Adam McAskill August 7, 2026 · 3 min read Certain types of dashboards tend to accumulate complexity. With that complexity, usability trends toward zero. Someone builds a useful report. More people start using it. Those people have different requirements, so the report gets a new filter, another tab and a few additional ways to group the data. This is often a good thing. The dashboard is becoming a richer reflection of how the business actually works. Eventually, though, it stops answering a defined set of questions and starts trying to contain a complex, branching analytical process in a single interface. The dashboard can notionally satisfy every requirement but, ugh, who wants to use it. Code helps, to a point Evidence handles this type of UI complexity particularly well because Evidence reports are defined in code. We offer UI primitives that simply don’t exist in legacy BI tools. Conditional blocks can reveal content only when it becomes relevant, based on the data or an input. Loops can generate focused views for different accounts, products or regions. Inputs can appear beside the content they control instead of being collected in a filter bar. These tools make it easier to manage cognitive load and keep a dashboard usable for longer. But even these affordances don’t scale forever. Enter skills In the Evidence Agent , each skill is a folder in the project repo. At its centre is a Markdown file called SKILL.md that describes how the agent should complete a particular type of analysis. Skills can include the questions the agent should ask and example queries, visualizations and generative UI to use in the response. They can point to reference material, invoke other skills, and even call out dashboards whose results or definitions the analysis must reconcile against. Users are no longer faced with the full complexity of the interface at once. The agent reads the skill, asks the relevant questions and guides them through the analysis. From there, the user can steer, backtrack or explore further as the results emerge. Because skills live in the repo, the data team can preview, test and deploy changes through the same development process as the rest of the Evidence project. From dashboard to skill One of our customers recently refactored their customer-health dashboard into a skill. The dashboard had started with one input: choose a customer. The first version showed product usage, support history and a renewal date. Over time it accumulated buying-group rollups, workspace-level results, onboarding cohorts, feature adoption and comparisons against previous contract periods. The dashboard encoded analytical patterns particular to the business, along with its visualization standards. There was a lot of valuable work in it. Using it, however, required knowing the customer-health methodology well enough to select the right inputs yourself. The skill can identify that an account belongs to a larger buying group and ask whether the user wants to review the group or one workspace. It can select the relevant comparison cohort, look for unusual changes and investigate which products and teams account for them before producing a focused report. The resulting skill is still a data product. It is version controlled, reviewed and improved over time. For users, it is much easier: they get the relevant analysis without navigating the entire procedure on a page. Refactoring is easy When your dashboards are already defined in code, coding agents can easily refactor them into skills. They can reuse the existing queries, definitions and visualizations, leaving you to simplify the dashboard or deprecate it entirely.

body_text: Researchers Discover Critical Time Windows That May Help Fight Glioblastoma More Effectively A new scientific study has revealed a promising approach that could transform the treatment of glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive and deadly forms of brain cancer. Researchers have identified specific periods immediately after brain tumor surgery when chemotherapy may work more effectively than under current treatment practices. The findings suggest that giving chemotherapy within minutes or a few days after surgery could improve drug delivery to the brain and potentially reduce the risk of the cancer returning. Although the research is still in its early stages and has not yet been tested in large human clinical trials, experts believe it could eventually change the standard approach to glioblastoma care. What Is Glioblastoma? Glioblastoma is the most aggressive type of brain tumor. It grows rapidly and often spreads into nearby brain tissue, making it extremely difficult to remove completely through surgery. Each year, approximately 3,200 people in the United Kingdom are diagnosed with glioblastoma. Unfortunately, survival rates remain very low, with only a small percentage of patients living five years or longer after diagnosis. Because microscopic cancer cells usually remain after surgery, the disease frequently returns even after patients receive chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Why Timing May Be the Key Current medical practice usually involves waiting four to six weeks after surgery before starting chemotherapy and radiation treatment. This delay allows patients time to recover from the operation. However, scientists from The University of Manchester believe there may be a better approach. Their research found that surgery temporarily disrupts the blood brain barrier, a protective layer that normally prevents many medicines from reaching brain tissue. During this brief period, chemotherapy drugs may gain better access to areas where cancer cells remain. Researchers identified two important treatment windows: Approximately 15 minutes after surgery. Around 48 to 72 hours following surgery. According to the study, delivering treatment during these periods could improve the effectiveness of cancer drugs before the blood brain barrier returns to its normal protective state. Understanding the Blood Brain Barrier The blood brain barrier acts as the body's natural defense system, protecting the brain from harmful substances circulating in the bloodstream. While this protection is essential for healthy brain function, it also creates a major obstacle for doctors trying to treat brain tumors. Many chemotherapy drugs cannot easily pass through this barrier, reducing their ability to reach cancer cells. The latest findings indicate that surgery temporarily creates an opportunity for medicines to cross into the brain more efficiently. Researchers believe this short period could become a valuable treatment window for future therapies. How the Study Was Conducted The research, published in Science Translational Medicine , used laboratory models designed to closely mimic the surgical removal of glioblastoma tumors. Scientists tested medicines that would normally struggle to enter the brain unless the blood brain barrier had been disrupted. The results showed that treatment delivered during the identified time windows significantly reduced tumor regrowth in the laboratory models. Although these findings are encouraging, researchers emphasize that additional studies involving human patients are necessary before this strategy becomes part of routine medical care. Expert Insights Lead researcher Dr. Thomas Kisby explained that the study demonstrates, for the first time, that glioblastoma surgery briefly creates a vulnerability that doctors may be able to use to their advantage. Researchers believe that carefully timed treatment during these periods could slow or even prevent the cancer from returning. Professor Kostas Kostarelos also noted that this strategy may allow doctors to use advanced therapies, including targeted medicines, nanoparticle treatments, immunotherapy, and gene therapy, more effectively after surgery. Instead of relying only on developing entirely new drugs, physicians may be able to improve outcomes by delivering existing treatments at the most beneficial time. Why This Research Matters Glioblastoma remains one of the most challenging cancers to treat because even the most successful surgeries cannot remove every cancer cell. Cancer cells that remain near the surgical site often begin growing again within months. If future clinical trials confirm these findings, doctors could introduce treatment much earlier than they do today, increasing the chances of destroying these remaining cancer cells before they spread. This approach could represent a major advancement in brain cancer treatment without necessarily requiring completely new medicines. Medical Experts Urge Caution Independent cancer specialists welcomed the research while stressing that it is still in its early stages. Experts say the findings provide valuable insight into improving drug delivery to the brain, but human clinical trials will be necessary before treatment guidelines can change. Researchers must confirm that earlier chemotherapy is both safe and effective for patients recovering from brain surgery. Only after successful clinical testing would hospitals consider updating current treatment protocols. Growing Calls for More Brain Cancer Research The publication of this study comes at a time when awareness of brain cancer is increasing across the United Kingdom. Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn, who was diagnosed with brain cancer at the age of 22, has recently urged the UK government to invest more heavily in brain cancer research and improve patient access to innovative clinical trials. His public appeal has highlighted the urgent need for greater funding, faster research, and improved treatment options for patients facing one of the deadliest forms of cancer. Symptoms of Glioblastoma Glioblastoma symptoms can vary depending on the location of the tumor but commonly include: Persistent headaches Memory problems Personality or behavior changes Difficulty speaking or understanding language Vision problems Weakness or numbness Extreme fatigue Seizures Nausea caused by increased pressure inside the skull Anyone experiencing persistent neurological symptoms should seek prompt medical evaluation. Looking Ahead While this breakthrough is not yet a cure, it offers hope for improving glioblastoma treatment in the future. The discovery that chemotherapy may work better during specific periods immediately after surgery opens new possibilities for doctors and researchers worldwide. Future clinical trials will determine whether these promising laboratory findings translate into improved survival and better outcomes for patients living with glioblastoma. If successful, this strategy could become an important step toward making one of the world's most difficult cancers more treatable. The research discussed is preliminary and requires further clinical testing before changes to standard treatment can be recommended. Patients should always consult qualified healthcare professionals regarding diagnosis, treatment options, and medical decisions.

body_text: For most passengers, flying is associated with holidays, business trips and long journeys across continents. For pilots and cabin crew, however, spending thousands of hours in the sky may involve a less visible occupational exposure: cosmic radiation. A new study examining mortality data from almost 13 million people across more than 500 occupations has highlighted concerns about radiation exposure among airline workers. The research suggests that pilots and flight attendants experienced the highest proportions of deaths from certain radiation-related cancers among the occupations examined. The findings, published in JAMA Internal Medicine , have renewed calls for stronger occupational protections for aircrew and closer monitoring of the risks associated with long-term exposure to cosmic radiation. Why are aircrew exposed to cosmic radiation? Radiation is present naturally in the environment, including high-energy particles that originate from space. Earth's atmosphere provides significant protection from this cosmic radiation, but that protection decreases as altitude increases. Commercial aircraft typically operate at altitudes where passengers and crew receive greater exposure to cosmic radiation than people at ground level. The amount can vary according to factors including flight altitude, duration and route. According to the study, US aircrew members receive an estimated 3 to 6 millisieverts of cosmic radiation annually. By comparison, the researchers estimated that an average traveller taking 10 cross-country return flights a year receives around 0.4 millisieverts. The difference is largely explained by frequency. A passenger may fly a handful of times each year, whereas professional aircrew can spend hundreds of hours in the aircraft environment. What did the researchers discover? Researchers analysed US death certificate data covering the period from 2020 to 2024. The dataset included occupational information that had only recently been linked to mortality records. In total, the analysis covered nearly 13 million deaths involving people from 503 occupations. Among those included were approximately 14,000 pilots and 7,000 flight attendants. The researchers considered several factors that can influence mortality, including age, sex, race, ethnicity, educational attainment and marital status. They examined deaths involving several cancers that can be associated with radiation exposure. These included breast cancer, cancers affecting the nervous system, leukaemia, lymphoma, thyroid cancer, prostate cancer and skin cancer. The analysis found statistically significant increases in mortality from breast cancer, central nervous system cancers, prostate cancer and melanoma among pilots and flight attendants. Pilots also showed a higher rate of death from leukaemia. One of the study's notable findings was that nearly 7 per cent of deaths among pilots and flight attendants were attributed to radiation-related cancers. The researchers said this proportion was higher than that observed among the other occupational groups included in their analysis, including nuclear technologists. Does this mean flying causes cancer? Not necessarily. The study identifies an association between aircrew occupations and cancer mortality. It does not establish that cosmic radiation was directly responsible for individual cancer cases or prove that flying caused those deaths. This distinction is important because occupational health research can involve many potential confounding factors. Aircrew members may have different sleep patterns, working schedules, reproductive histories, lifestyle factors and other occupational exposures compared with people working on the ground. The researchers themselves highlighted limitations in the analysis. Occupations recorded on death certificates may sometimes be incorrectly classified, while the available data did not provide detailed information about the precise radiation exposure experienced by each individual. As a result, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of a potential occupational health concern rather than proof of a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Why might pilots and cabin crew face different risks? The most obvious factor is repeated exposure. A long-haul pilot or flight attendant may spend a substantial portion of their working life at cruising altitude. Over years or decades, relatively small exposures accumulated across thousands of hours could become more significant. Cosmic radiation also varies depending on flight conditions. Higher altitudes generally provide less atmospheric shielding, while routes at higher latitudes can experience greater exposure because of differences in Earth's magnetic protection. This means that radiation exposure is not necessarily identical for every member of an airline workforce. What could stronger protection look like? The researchers argue that occupational radiation protections for aircrew should reflect the levels of exposure they experience. That could involve better systems for estimating individual cumulative exposure, improved occupational monitoring and clearer guidance for workers and employers. Airlines could also consider radiation exposure when planning crew schedules and routes, particularly for workers who regularly operate long-haul or high-altitude services. The goal would not necessarily be to prevent people from flying. Instead, better measurement could help employers understand which workers receive the greatest cumulative exposure and support evidence-based occupational health measures. What does the research mean for passengers? For the occasional traveller, the findings are unlikely to mean that ordinary air travel should be viewed as a major cancer risk. The researchers' estimates show a substantial difference between the exposure experienced by professional aircrew and that of typical passengers. Someone who flies occasionally spends far less time at altitude than someone whose career involves flying every week. Frequent flyers may receive more exposure than occasional travellers, but the occupational situation of pilots and cabin crew is fundamentally different because of the cumulative number of hours spent at altitude throughout a career. The study is therefore primarily relevant to occupational health rather than routine holiday travel. A growing occupational health question The latest research adds to previous studies suggesting that aircrew may experience higher rates of certain cancers than the general population. What makes this analysis notable is its focus on mortality across a very large number of occupational groups. The researchers said the pattern observed among pilots and flight attendants was not seen in the same way for non-radiation-related cancers or among ground-based aviation workers. They concluded that the findings support an association between cumulative in-flight cosmic radiation exposure and several radiation-related cancers. However, more research will be needed to establish the precise relationship between exposure and cancer outcomes. Future studies could benefit from detailed occupational histories, individual flight records and more accurate estimates of cumulative radiation exposure. Such information could help researchers distinguish the effects of cosmic radiation from other factors associated with working in aviation. What happens next? The central issue is not whether people should stop flying. Aviation remains one of the world's most important forms of transport, connecting countries and communities every day. Instead, the research raises a question about how occupational health protections should evolve as scientists learn more about the long-term effects of working at altitude. Pilots and cabin crew spend far more time exposed to cosmic radiation than ordinary passengers. The new findings suggest that this difference deserves closer attention, particularly for workers who accumulate thousands of flight hours over their careers. The study does not prove that cosmic radiation caused the cancers recorded among aircrew members. It does, however, provide further evidence of an association that researchers believe warrants greater occupational monitoring and protection. For airline workers, the message is therefore one of awareness rather than alarm. Better exposure measurement, continued medical research and appropriate workplace safeguards could help determine how aviation employers should manage this unusual but potentially important occupational hazard. Source: The Independent, reporting on research published in JAMA Internal Medicine , 18 August 2026.
